blocks.x: I want you to feel as if you know me 59 years. Alright. Of course I'm only 39 years old. Jack Benny and I. This is my chair. This is where I sit and look at the TV. And lately I haven't been getting Channel 4, so I called Burt. He's in the TV business now since he's got his children growing up. He doesn't play much music. He's a Saturday nighter.
That's Burt Andrews.
Burt. He plays sax and clarinet. Entirely neglected by Sushaw and company in that book.
And he's Dutch's brother?

Dutch's brother. You know, it would take the whole book to tell my story. I know. But I made a terrible mistake. Now understand that I respected Dr. Sushaw and he was my friend. I played for his daughter's supper dance when she was queen of the carnival. I knew his wife when she was a young girl, Mari Estupa, her name was. And he was publishing the second line and I was a member of the jazz club. And I tend to join again. I have the application. But I'm waiting until January. Why give him $10 for December? December. Yeah. And Steve Larkana is a friend of mine. We worked together at the Sanger. And Steve is an officer. So I went down there the other night. What a mob that was. Whew! But they had a colored band. It was very good. St. Augustine. Mm-hmm. Hostel band, yeah. Oh, I'll tell you, those boys, whoever's in tune, that's the main thing with me. I can listen to a straight melody and if it's a tune, it's all right with me, it passes my stuff. You don't have to be too fancy. My wife used to like Benny Goodman when he played straight. You know, I wanted to ask you something. I wanted to ask you something.
I want you to ask you something. Are you sure? Yeah, sure.
Yeah. He's picking us both up.
All right. Why don't you name your name? Yeah. I'd like to get your full name down.

My name is John G-O-H-N, capital D-E, capital D-R-O-I-T, Good Rock. And the middle name? No middle name. In my family there were two uncles who had money. One was named John and one was named Paul. And in the whole family you find nothing but John and Paul. That's what you call a coincidence.
You call that ignorance. They used to speak French so I couldn't understand them.

When I went to high school, the professor, your mother's a solitary, your father's a good guy, you don't speak French, you're a disgrace to the French race. I thought I'm an American, I'm not a Frenchman. But that didn't do any good. But he was too good for boys, I went to school, he had no name. Just call boys, hi.

Let me get my name and Betty's name done. Betty, can you give yours? This is Betty Rankin. Yeah, and I'm Dick Allen. And I'm Tom Hedley Droid. So we all know each other's name and we have that on the tape.
Just looking at you, you were kindred spirits.
No, I was the world's worst musician. That's why I quit. But I'm glad to know about your family background.

Well, my father was a musician, my brother was the greatest drummer I ever lived. He was with Alfred Newman for many years. And Hollywood. I have the red book that Soussone got out, it says that he played in the pit at the Orphiom and with his brother Johnny's band. He was the greatest woodpile man on the Pacific coast. You know the woodpile, the marimbas, huh? And he had Georgia the drum section. He made enough money to retire in three figures. He had the drawing account $15,000 a year if he never had a note. But he knew the business. He started with Flip the Frog, the cartoons. They eventually went out of business, but my brother got to be quite a sound effect man. He was a great band and he loved learning his own. In addition to being a great drummer, because he played big time at 16, he was also a trombonist. And he could read all the clefs and all the keys. He was a musician.
I didn't know he was a trombonist.

I never heard of him. My brother was a trombonist. I played the violin fairly well, enough to double. And I attempted piano, just for the harmony, you know. But I had the finest trumpet teacher in the world. He was a member of the Republican Guard Band of France. He came here with the French Opera Company. And my father believed in good instruction. And I got it.
And his name?

Pardon? P-A-U-L-I-N. F-A-B-I-A-N. Fabian. Fabian. I made my first professional engagement when I was 12, standing on the Coca-Cola box, playing at a mass meeting, political meeting. I got eight dollars. I was a rich man that night.
Since we're mentioning dates, if you're eight years old, do you know your brother's birthday? Yes.
My brother was born October 24th, 1894. I was born December the 4th, 1892. So?
I'm 77 years ago.
Today.
So we know what today is. Happy birthday again. Thank you very much.

I appreciate that. I've been getting in all day. I've got some beautiful neckties. And they did it. They're those wide babies. I've been in obscurity for the last five years. I've had a lot of luck. My poor wife was sick for over four years. I didn't leave the house once at night in four years. I have a car that's six years old. It only has 22,000 miles on it. I missed my fishing. I had no golf. Because when I'd get up in the morning, I'd tend to her as well as good. And then the cook would come and she'd fix the breakfast and eat breakfast. And then I had to go out and get supplies. I had to buy the meat and stuff. And do a lot of other things for a woman who was so used to doing for herself that she used to wish that God would take her every morning. She suffered tortures. She died in the Providence house. You know, by the two-year-old. It's a beautiful place. Providence house.
I've passed it. Well, it's beautiful.

If the rates are a little bit out on some people, but with Medicare you can make a go of it. You know, Medicare has been very kind of me because those doctors let you have a friend, I'm telling you. Although Ted Block is a fine doctor. Has a good heart. So what you see, you see me with wide trousers on, but I can show you some. Now I try. My daughter is the one. Well, she's up to date. She's a beautiful girl. She was here this morning. She wants her daddy to be just so. And her friends, that's why I'm living in Georgia. And I might, in my ignorance, I may have taken a room on Camp Street. But she made the lineup from the Arlene all the way down. She said, Daddy, your friends, most of your friends are in the Georgian, which they are. I mean, friends and customers and people who helped to make me. My contemporaries.
And they all know me.
I'm getting invites all around.
I come in and have a cup of coffee. Were you born here in the city?

Born and raised in New Orleans. Spent a lot of time. I was pleased. Elsewhere, I had my band in New York. I toured with Arnold Johnson under the name of Paul Whiteman's orchestra, which was a misnomer. But we, they only took us because we were too good. We were playing at Martin's Casino in Atlantic City when they heard the band. And Whiteman must have said, I better get this band under my wing. And he did. He also took in the red caps. So I was playing at the Grunewal at the time. And Mr. Grunewal, do you know where the Grunewal is? That's the President Roosevelt Hotel. Yeah. Well I was playing in the cave. I have a clipping. I took a picture of the cave. Guess who was on the back of it? Fuzzola. I didn't know it. Remember the great Fuzzola?
Oh I knew him slightly.

Oh he did. He played with me a long time. He played with me for nine months on the jungle roof. I used to get the summer job at the White House at the Buena Vista. Those were the jobs that made music, just free share of stock in a golf club. That helps doesn't it?
Oh yeah.

A cottage and room and board for you and your wife and your daughter. Everybody's catering to you. You know what I mean? It's wonderful. And fishing. When I heard about Biloxi being damaged, it hurt me. I got sick. Of course that Biloxi was not the Biloxi that I knew. There was only one gambling joint near Biloxi. I think it was 12 miles out on the Isle of Caprice they call it. And it went down and sunk out. I went there once and I didn't have a coat on. They wouldn't let me in the gambling place. But the fella said, we have a coat. If I stayed there much longer, I wouldn't have had a coat or anything else. But I've had a full life.
That's wonderful. And your father you say was a master?

My father, yes he was. He was a band master of the first Texas Regiment of Volunteer Infantry. Doing the Spanish American law. He says he helped to fill up all the holes and clean all the wilderness. Cuba and Florida. He came back. He had three trades. None of which he liked. He wanted to be a musician. And he afterwards had his own band. It was a military band. And he was slightly successful. But not enough to raise my brother and I. So he opened a store. He gave the proper weight. And sold good stuff and retired in 12 years. Which was pretty good, huh?
Oh yeah.

And he always wanted me to be the best. He wanted me to be what he was. I remember I was going to Bois High School. I have pictures that show you when I was 14 years of age. I act, there was, where the telephone company's office now stands on Barone Street was known as Brooks Wintergarten. And I happened to have one of the programs and my good friend, Yuba, oh he'd leave that. I gave him a lot of stuff that they wouldn't know anything about. Because I was just, and I'm not a man who writes down the names and dates. My dad was like that. So I made it hard for everybody because I had to dig back to find out. I'll have to look for a snapshot that maybe I put on it because it was my wife or somebody. And I'd get to the gate. If you asked me when I played at the Green Mill Gardens in Chicago, I'd have to look up the evidence although I played there. But I don't have much of a memory for dates. At this age I don't have much to remember except tunes.
You never forget those.

Never forget music. I love music. My father gave me a trumpet when I was 10 years of age. He went off and came back that afternoon and I played America for him. On the trumpet. I don't know, I must have had a natural ambiture. Because right now I can just get about eight notes out of my horn and I can't practice here. And I'm not going to run to the shrine just because anyone. I have other things to do, things that I would like to do. But I would love to play my trumpet again. But if I couldn't play it the way I want to play it, I'm not going to play it. Because they want me to take the stick. I remember I went on vacation to Miami with my wife and my mother-in-law and his wife. They lived in Daytona. So our pastor was in Daytona and took them to freedom of Miami. And the wife and I, we went to Havana because they didn't want to go out there had been. So they stayed in Miami. Havana was a beautiful place there. And I came back. So coming back to New Orleans, we stopped in Biloxi and we went in Barachefs because they had Abbey Bruness in there. Have you heard of Abbey Bruness? I heard him there. Great, great jazz man. George Bruness' brother. Merrick Bruness played trombone. Loud trombone, but good, but good. And Henny, I called him Henny, his name was Henry. He played in the district, the red light district. He could play more with his feet than some people could play with their hands. He used to put his foot up in the slide. And I'm telling you, I loved it. I was brought up as a legit musician. I played in New Orleans Symphony on the fresh air, but for all egotistical reasons, just to prove that I could. You know musicians are egotists. They love to play it, but when I played in the Alfie Theater, success came to me from the Alfie Theater. And I mean suddenly, and money. Of course I was getting a good salary at the Alfie Theater. I was getting $86 a week. I was married and we got a loan fine and all that. You know, we didn't have to pay much money. And my brother was my biggest booster. And one day we were playing the weekly, and I don't know whether they were dying or had a funeral, but Tasso was playing some old tune that only Emil Tasso, who was our greatest vaudeville leader. You've heard of him. His son is still living. We play a tune like that, but the changes, they lay natural for me. So my brother says, get with it. I say, what do you mean? He says, put the mute in and let him have it. And Tasso didn't expect it. It almost hit him in the head when I put the mute in and I started to do it nice and quiet. And they had a beautiful set of strings. We had two first violins, a viola, a shell and a bass that were out of this world. I got those full chords, the flute and the clarinet, they didn't intrude. And the trombonist was my sidekick. He didn't play at all because he didn't want to cover me. The tune was called China We All Out To You. Did you ever hear that tune? Never. I have never heard it since. Well, when I stopped, when we stopped, the house came down in the darkness. And then so on, I had to have something ready, which made it a hard job, 52 weeks in a week. But I have some write-ups that repay me. I have a write-up that says, with the exception of my trumpet playing, there was nothing in the show. How do you like that? And I saved it and I can show it to you.
Did they put a spotlight on you?
No, I'm in the dark.
In the dark?

Weekly, the news is going on. It's the news. I'm thinking of a guy in a theater. That music, Tassel never did. When I was a leader of the Liberty Theater, I had to feature my own pictures. I had to sit there with my first violinist and he'd have a tap. And I'd say, the theme this week, I'd pick out a nice theme for two lovers to clinch. We used to have a first and second theme, secondary theme. And I'd always close the curtain with my theme. And I'd talk it over with the manager who was a palomar. I'd say, how much of the feature do you want me to play? He'd say, you're going to play the first 30 minutes. So we'd sit there for 30 minutes. What went on in the middle, I never could tell you. I never used to look at it. But I directed some fine pictures. I directed way down east, Three Musketeers, Four Horsemen of the Apocalypse. You ever heard of them? I've heard of them. They were from Griffith, the road show pictures. They sent you a book. You had nothing to worry about except to have the musicians to play it. See? And then they'd put a screen up in front of it so they wouldn't know how few or how many we had behind it. But I usually insisted and got what I needed. If I needed a nobel player, I got one. Because they controlled the music. It was the singer that afterwards became Paramount Richards. And I was in the staff. I had to go along with them lots of times when I didn't want to go, but I was always secure. You know, musicians' life is not always the better roses, you know. They have weeks when they don't wake, you know. Got a long show of short. I was out of one day in eleven years. Is that a record?
I know you must have played in a lot of different kind of places to do that. No.

Four years in Grunewald and seven years at Cobb's, Cobb's Tea Room. Eleven to one at night. We didn't get six sets in. We'd get a beer and get three sets and the night's over. And then when we had competitions with the other places trying to put us out of business, they brought in acts. And Mr. Cobb knew as much about running a nightclub as I knew about flying an airplane. He'd have a bill of fare that... I said, Mr. Cobb, we need a bill of fare that big with sandwiches. Find out what they're drinking. All the college kids brought orange aid for ninety cents and sat there all night with it. Friday night we had to take the tablecloths off the table. They'd take everything out of the place. But we had the young people and that's what people like. People like young people. Old people like young people. I like the old people because they spend their money. But I worked the first two weeks in Cobb. They cut out the music in the Grunewald and Mr. Cobb had been after me. So I went home and I said, Mr. Cobb, we're through. He said, why? I said, we're just through. I said, now's your chance to get a hold of us. Why not open the tea room? Because he had tried it with several orchestras and they didn't draw their breath. He said, the place is not in condition and we were in Lent. 19th of March. I said, Mr. Cobb, I'll bring you enough masons and Jews to pack the place. Don't worry about the Catholics with the Lent. He said, what do you mean? I said, I have the clientele. I have the follower. And I did. I don't mind telling you. I'd stand in front of the cats and best off on Canal Street and see anybody come and say,
I haven't seen you.

Where you been? Well, he said, it's only so he made a table. It got so we didn't have enough tables and the head waiter started making all the money. Because my friends would say, you asked me to come. He tells me I don't have a table. And I had made the reservations for them. So I told Mr. Cobb, I want to know who he'd wear them. I practically ran that joint because he knew nothing about it. All he did was sit there and smoke, chain smoking cigars, you know. Fine man, finest. Could have lost a short, I waited for seven years without a contract, which was to my advantage. Because every time I got an offer from New York, Chicago or Birmingham, better than his, I'd show it to him. I can't beat that. I'd say, what can you do?

There was a trumpet player there that I never have been able to find much about. And I thought maybe he was there right before you or right after you. Did you know Frank Garante? He was from Italy. Frank who?

Garante? Great. Frank Garante. Frank Garante. Which I say he was my contemporary. I've been a little ahead of him. Frank lived up at Exposition Boulevard magazine. He had an apartment there. I lived on a camp between Henry P. and Webster, which is close together. And we used to play duets together. And he played an Italian trumpet with the side action, you know.
Rotary valves or regular?
Rotary valves, like a French horn.
He had a beautiful tone.

He had a big tone. He played fine. And he played in comms for the dinner session. That was after, I must have migrated when he got in there because I used to own the place. I had the dinner session, the lunch session, the night session. I can show you programs where my name is on everything that's in the city, in the neighborhood. Well, I hustle. Many times my wife would talk about my daughter being sick and stuff. She'd say, you wouldn't know, you were never home. I said, no. I said, those $65 dresses would be nice, don't they? I'd be over in Biloxi and there's a dozen dresses over there. What am I going to do? I've got to get left. She has to have some amusement. And she had amusement. See? I couldn't let that stop me because music was my life. And she was my life. I was married to a fifth. You're going to take this? Well, it is. It is.
It's going.
No, no.
No, no. No, no. No, no. I'll tell you later. I'll cut it out if you want to.
This is a little too personal. She just died recently.
Well, anything you want to cut out, we can cut out.

Yeah. Well, she's... I'm the only man she ever knew. I met her when she was 14. Her mother wouldn't let me take her out. And when I did take her out, I had to take her sister. And everybody wanted to know whether I was calling her or her sister, because they were equally beautiful. And I'll say she was beautiful. She's half English and half German. She was a natural blonde. She had a little bit dark. She never did blue or anything. My wife looked at she was fine at 50, and some women looked at 30. Despite of the fact that she had six operations. Donovan Brown kept her alive. I thank him a whole lot. I kept her until she was 74.
And you had children too, you mentioned. I have a... A daughter?
I have a gorgeous daughter. She's good looking. She's on the ball up to date. She has a beautiful moment. She knows what to do and how to do it. And I'm proud about it.
Is this your granddaughter's picture on the wall? That is my granddaughter.
That was what you... This is your granddaughter.
Well that must be your great... That's my great granddaughter. She's...

I didn't bring my wife's picture. I didn't bring my wife's picture because I hid them and I can't find them. It makes me feel too blue. Especially sitting in this room by myself. If you go out to my daughter's, you see my wife. I was proud of my wife in Biloxi. I used to have to beat those jelly beans off. You know you used to call a young fellow jelly beans. I'd say sweetheart I want you to dance, but I want you to dance with those I want you to dance with. So tell them to ask me. So they come up and say would you like your dance? Beautiful girl. Beautiful clothes. Sitting there by myself. She'd say you'll have to ask my husband. He's the leader of the band. And sometimes they didn't have nerve enough. But I knew all the nice boys. I thought I did anyhow. I'd say well you saved me. Because I wanted them to have some fun. You know that's not some... You'd be all dressed and nowhere to go you know. Because that was only three hours. She forgot the other 21 hours that you live like a queen you know. You didn't have to wash or dish or anything. And they walked in and me catering to her. One hundred percent. That's... She used to buy clothes from a shop called the Harold Shop. It was in the Roosevelt. And he was a smart boy. He'd sell them a box of dresses. They'd never go back. He'd give them all. He knew what she... He said if he ever needed a model she would be... I said no she wouldn't. But he said I mean I would like to have them.
You know. So...
Things a little dreary now. But they'll pick up.
You didn't have any sons to carry on in music? I had no sons to carry on.

My daughter is an excellent pianist. My wife was an excellent pianist. I remember... And this is way back. When this... Armistice Day... Now I am going back. Armistice Day? World War One? Yeah. Mr. Gruenwald said... Not Mr. Weiss. Mr. Gruenwald. The Gruenwald said... Johnny! If possible get the band together. I said it's the middle of the day. He said well get them... Get something. We're going to have a celebration here. Armistice is having to sign at 11 o'clock. I'd like to hear the band at 12 o'clock. Well I worked fast. I dug up everybody but the piano. So I asked Mrs. D. Duarte to play the piano for me. And she's sitting up there in a powder blue dress with a big powder blue hat. You know how to dress in the old days. And all the girls come up throwing their arms around my neck with my wife sitting at the piano.
I said that's Armistice Day.

You know? Well then after a while in comes my piano player, Tom Zimmerman, one of the greatest, I can't tell you how great he was and couldn't read a note as big as a customer. When he played he was Frankie Call and another Frankie Call. My idea of a rhythm piano player, I mean clean playing, was Frankie Call. Did you ever hear Frankie Call? Sure. Didn't he have a touch? Beautiful. And melodic too.
That's what I mean.

I mean I'm like Louis Armstrong and I'm a contemporary. I helped him when he had patches in his pants. I helped many a colored man. I remember, I know he published Don't Mean a Thing If You Ain't Got That Swing, because I played the first three of them, Clarence Williams. And when I went to New York to play at Healy's Balkanades, and he called me up and he said, Johnny I've got some new tunes and they just fit you, and if you don't mind I'll come to rehearsal and tell you how I think they should be played. Not that I want to teach you, but what I did, I heard about the tunes. So he brought Don't Mean a Thing and He Didn't Get That Swing. And there was another band that thought they were good. Well I was a featured band and they played while we rested, so you know, it was secondary. They didn't have the right instrumentation. They had a fiddle, a trumpet and a saxophone, the loudest I've heard of my life, and a toothless drummer. Well they didn't make the appearance. I was always for the stiff shirt tuxedo and the week time. My band was impeccable. I'll show you pictures, you'll see some nice looking fellas. But they could play. Like Meyer Weinberg, you remember Meyer Weinberg?
Yes.
He calls himself Gene Meyer now.
I've never met him, I've heard him on the record.

Oh boy, he played the chorus, stay in your own backyard on the saxophone, and she'd go down for posterity. And I had Joseph Larkana who died not long ago, his name was Erasmus, but he called himself Joe, he didn't like the name Erasmus. He only had one lady.
Yes, the alto player, saxophone.

At that time, he was with me, I'll show you the picture. And I had Eddie Powers who was in the man always on time. I had a fine band. I had Tony Almarico as my hot man. And Red Bowman as my first trumpet player. Wyatt Sharp as my trabumpa. He's not on the Jerry L.A. Do you know him?
No, I don't know him.
He has a man in Jackson, Mississippi.
What is his name? Wyatt Sharp.

W-Y-A-T-T-S-H-A-R-P. I didn't know him. He played with me at Suburban Gardens, and he was a very bright man. He managed by hook or crook, by leaving his clothes in his locker after Suburban Gardens, that he slept two nights in the Roosevelt and paid for one. Yeah, that's the truth. Because he was on the Donbusters, you see. He played with Pinky on the Donbusters. So he'd move in and leave a call for Donbusters, six o'clock, and he'd move out. Because most of his clothes and his tucks were in the locker at the nightclub. And how he did it, I don't know. He lived at the Roosevelt for 30 nights, slept there 30 nights and paid for 15. That's how smart he was. So he went up to Jackson, organized his own band, and he took two names and made one name out of it and called himself Jerry Lane. And I heard his band. And unfortunately for me, the night that I heard his band, we were both playing in the same place and I had a six piece Dixieland combination because I took all kinds of jobs, you know, for money. And I didn't. I don't think I sounded too good because I know he had, he had been great, but you can't carry a whole band on your shoulders, you know. That's why when I got a good man, I kept him. And my dad said to me, never break up a winning combination. Many times I want to change. He says, is the boy doing a good job? I said, good. Don't break up a winning combination. And I always tried to be nice, I gave a good job, played plenty of music. I always let them know the tune I was playing too. Don't forget that. Like Louis says, I like to hear the tune I'm playing. I had to impress on me about arrangements because I used to have a lot of arrangements, good arrangements, but the way the music used to come out, you wouldn't have time. So I'd take the stocks and I'd trick them up. And other band leaders thought I was playing special. Because they used to come on the boat when I played on the boat. I played on the president. It was one series of arguments between the captain and I. I said to him one night, I said, Captain Stratfuss, I said, I honor you and I respect you. But why don't you run the band and let me run the boat? Which captain was this? Captain Stratfuss, Captain Roy, the old man. He'd keep handing me programs from St. Louis. I said, we are playing in New Orleans. We're not playing in St. Louis. I don't want to know what they're playing in St. Louis. I'm playing and I don't change my style for a month on the boat. I said, he says, well, they do say you give good, honest music. I said, no one has to tell me that I know it. And I said, your advisors, one of them particularly, couldn't get past the first inning when he tried to play with me. Couldn't even tell a chapter about me, I'd throw them overboard. Then he said, the same guy, and you mentioned his name a while ago. He's my friend now, we're friends, because he helped me collect a collection of Armstrong records. It was priceless. My little, my granddaughter knocked it off her table and ruined most of them. I almost died. I'm so hard. But Dutch Andrews helped me get the collection. But Dutch, well in order to strengthen himself, he'd give advice. Who was he to give advice? So I said, Captain, you run the band. I'll run the boat. We're both right up on the rocks. He wouldn't let me play at V&E's walls. I said, Captain, I cater through the years to different people, different clientele than you have. Not that I'm a snob, but I play for the richest. I play for carnival balls, supper dances, conventions. Why was I the number one band for MCA here for years? Why did, I didn't have to bid on jobs. Why did they say, are you available? And when I send the prices, he said, Johnny, we can't make any money with you. I said, why? You don't charge. He said, you don't charge enough. For instance, I remember years ago, it impressed me so that people, people like to get robbed. I bid on a Coca-Cola, imagine that the Edwards, that's another place. I can show you a letter with the man, you think I was just stunned, how he praises me. I bid $350 for Coca-Cola, and MCA gets me on the phone, Johnny, can you play Coca-Cola? I said, yes. I said, but I already bid on them. What did you bid? I said, $350. He said, no good. I said, how much? He said, $900. I ride back a variable, $900 in my car. Now how do you like that? For people like that. And the same man didn't even remember me. I said, I'm not going to buy a car. He didn't even remember me. He must have thrown my letter. You see the edgewater-
You think the band wasn't any good when you bid $350?

Well, MCA, like everybody else, would give you a throw off of Tommy Darcy, and wind up with Joe McGluck, and that's who you got. You know what I mean? But the edgewater, Mr. Shoemaker had been a bellboy when I played at the White House. He loved me, he liked me, he knew I played good music, and he knew he could trust me. Just the same as Seymour Weiss told me, Johnny, when you own that band stand, you represent me. Because I remember one night the headweather got smart because I didn't ask him if I could play overtime. I said, I'll play overtime with anybody if they pay me. And especially if they're friends like the National Cocknoseed Compress Association, wouldn't think of any other band but mine and spend maybe $20,000, $50,000 on a Roosevelt, I'm going to ask that maitre d', he should take a walk, let him get these waiters don't love them. So he starts to get smart and the band's looking at me all up, they're upset that I should take abuse, because I never did take abuse from anybody. After I got enough I said, look I had enough out of you, one more out of you and I'll bust you in the nose. And the band said, Johnny wins! And they all hold their hair up. Don't put that down, because the band's retired.
But I've had something in the situation.
I've had some bad, some bad moments, but that one, I let him talk his head off. But maybe I get abusive.

I was 16, I used to play golf with his dad and his dad kept telling me about him so I hit him in an audition and he floored me. Charlie Luckow? Charlie Luckow. His father was a fine gentleman, he died early in life, he was the head of a finance company. Charlie will tell you, I was talking to Charlie the other day. See I'm dead to lots of those fellas. Bob Young, my first sax man, I took him in the union when he was 16. And now there's nobody like me and I'm worried about him because he's not too well. I sent him to Dr. Brown, I hope Dr. Brown finds out what's wrong with him because his sister died at 23 with cancer.
Well who was this Cooper fella?
Who?
You said it was a Cooper fella at the Grand Hotel? Oh boy. Yeah.

Pat Cooper played bass for him. At the Grand, he plays with the accordionist who also played with me at various times. Of course in my career of over 40 years as a leader I had a lot of different musicians, but always had the best I hope. Some of whom maybe were not considered the best by some other man leaders who were ignorant. They didn't know that you had to have a man who could play a floor show, you know? I played for Dick Shawn, I didn't know him for Madame, he throws me the books. I say Dick Shawn, well he'll phrase me, he'll do notes. He did it in about an hour and a half. I didn't rehearse him, 45 minutes. It would take Ed Sullivan all week to rehearse him. I played his show. He says I know you now, you're Johnny. I said how you know me? He says the spotlight man told me that you would have preached the trumpet at the Orpheus. I said you're going back in the prehistoric days. He says but that shows me that you have the experience. And I played his act and he just hugged me and I thanked him. I didn't ask for testimonials, I didn't hear the thing. But I know Dick Shawn, same way when I played the Four Freedoms Show, when they were selling bombs, they brought down that handsome fellow, who was that ladies man, that good looking actor, he's been years going by. And you see I'll tell you my memory goes back. Well I knew show better, so I played everything from the Monkeys to Grand Opera. And one show I had to lay off I sent Russ Papalia because Russ Papalia was my protege. Russ formerly played trombone in my band. And when I hired Russ he almost faded because it's your band. I said Russ you play a good solid trombone, you play the spots. And naturally being vain I didn't want any trombone to play a cover of me on people with
the drums.
Well I was a leader. So I put Russ there, I went to show and I came back. Billy DeWolf, Billy DeWolf. You've heard of him?
Yes.

I'll get the other fella's name, he was a ladies man from Taw, he was a handsome fellow, a leading man. And Billy DeWolf looks down at the pit and he tells that huge audience, I felt like a millionaire. He says it is certainly a pleasure to see Johnny Dread back in the pit. He missed me so much. Because his motions and his actions were strictly more of them. You know he's an old timer. They call him Mr. Billy DeWolf now. Well I mean all that makes you feel good. Like I can recite that writer where the man says, it was mighty nice to see Johnny back in the pit with his triumphant trumpet. That's a good word, that. Triumphant trumpet. And with that exception there was nothing of merit in his show. Now I'm sure they cost thousands of dollars. You think that I would, his son, Emel Washburn, he just loved me. He died. Have you heard of Emel Washburn? I've heard of him. I don't know. He was a theatrical writer. KTK, did you ever hear of him? He had acid on his tongue. They were all afraid of him. They were all afraid of him. And when they knew that KTK was in the front, I don't think they could do that. But what did New Orleans mean? They had a week in New Orleans and gone. But never had an acid touch for me. He said someday they're going to realize they got something. You know?
I was wondering about your records and Russ Papalia. He played trouble with me on the records.

But I would say here and now there is nothing of distinction attached to my records. I made a terrible mistake. A man came down here. No, I had a friend, Mr. Peer. He was a man that was doing his own piano house. And he was friendly with, no, I'm going to get the names all wrong. Mr. Peer was the president of OK Records. He played a fair golf game. And he played a fair golf game. But he thought he played a better one. So I let him win the second nine. First thing your secretary says, Mr. Peer beat you on the second nine. I said, let me touch him. I'm going to beat him with one o'clock. We used to have to cross the river, go under the tunnel, get a trolley car, jump on a steam train. I don't know where we went to play golf around New York. I'm talking about New York.
Yeah. But he liked me. He made my kid.
You want to get it going again? Okay.

Yeah, it's all right. I would rather it be known because I, truthfully, in spite of the fact that I thought he was more or less a mountainebank, now that's not a good thing to say, but he wasn't a musician he was talented to be, and he couldn't sing a lick, but he thought he could. But he was the finest gentleman you ever met. His whole heart was in music, and he liked me, and I turned on him. Only in this respect, that when he asked me for an interview, I said, what's the matter, you ran out of Negroes? Because of the second line, it'd be Negro, Negro, Negro, Negro. No Johnny Detroit, no Tony Parenti, no, you know. From then on, he disliked me. Well, when my brother died, he came to the house with a tape recorder. We discussed my brother's life. I tried to get him as much as I could, and I have copies of it if I can find it. I'd be glad to let you read it. He wrote the finest obituary of my brother that any man could possibly, well written, beautifully written, and praised my brother to the highest. But after this incident with me, in discussing my brother in his book, he says that Paul Detroit played in the Orphian Pitman with his brother Johnny's band. And my brother played with the finest officers, with Johnny Green, played with Alfred Newman. So, I didn't get to love Doc much anymore. But I was wrong. I was wrong. If Doc was alive, I would tell him I was wrong, and I told him I was wrong when he was alive. But I must have heard it. And I'm sorry. Because I could have left that unsaid.
Well, it may not have been his fault, you know. It may have been some pressure put on him by the publishers or something of the book.

No, he... No, the book didn't... This... Durrell Black. Wasn't it Durrell Black? No, it was with Al Rose. I know. They sent me a testimonial, and I'm a jazzy model, and my daughter has his frame. I guess they sent out a million of them, because Dr. Block says, I'm waiting until you see you come out. You never came out. I said, I don't leave the house at night, Dr. Block. I said, I have a sick wife, because you know you're treating her, you know. Well, this... My daughter's so proud of it, she had it framed in it. She gives lots of court parties, and has lots of friendships. It's a topic of discussion, that I am a jazzy model. Why did they make me a jazzy model when I was in the business? I'm great now. Everybody knows the great John McIndra. But when I was in the business, I had to hustle like the rest of them. You mean, huh? Everybody... Every musician has his ups and downs. I didn't have any downs. I always prepared for the rainy day, because I... I never gambled. And I bought property. When the pressure came, I was land poor. But that's why I can live here. Don't worry what I'm going to eat. Ask for no favors. And I didn't buy any clothes all the while. My wife was sick. I bought two complete suits, and a board coat, and trousers, and that yesterday. Because my daughter said, Daddy, you don't have to dress that way. I don't care how... I have fallen away, I went down. But I look clean. I'm always clean. And my band was always impeccable. It took me a lot to let them wear soft shirts with a tuxedo. But I found out how good it was. When I went to work at the Greenville Garden, I'm the only man in the band with a stiff shirt. And I had a weak car. Charlie McNeil, the world's greatest band choice at that time, he was the first man to write the chord systems. You know, chord walking, you go... Yes, I played with him. In fact, he was a piano repair man for all the ballad and the cat's theaters, and the trombone player was the mechanic. He'd go there and condemn the pianos and the trombone player would repair them. He had a beautiful racket. I'm telling you right now. He whispers in my ear one night, Johnny, don't answer me. I said, what? Isham Jones wants to see you. Remember Isham Jones? No. He was playing at the Rainbow Gardens down the street. I'm playing at the Greenville. Wood gets around, there's a guy at the Greenville, he can play the trumpet. Isham Jones wants to get a hold of me. But I'm important. The union had known it, they had thrown me out bodily. I was brought... The way I made my entrance into the Greenville Gardens, I went there one night, put my trumpet in the bar, sat at the table and listened to the band. I walked up to Johnson. He knows all about it. He's in coach with the boss. I said, I see you don't have a trumpet. You know, you quit. I said, I'm a trumpet player. I said, where are you from? I said, New Orleans, he knows all about it. New Orleans. When you say New Orleans, it's made. It's made. And you better be hot. I said, may I sit in? He said, sure. Get your horn. Where's your horn? I said, the horn is on the bar. So I get the horn, I take it out, I sit down. He said, where do you want to play? I said, anything. Well, I went for the musicians. He said, anything. Well, you know what to pick out. Pick out a couple of standards. You know Dixieland standards. Not having any trumpet. I saw like ten trumpets. And I played well. I had the job in the pot. Because the boss had wanted me his car and his chauffeur to find me an apartment. He used to give me a beer at the cost. And the luckiest thing after going all over Chicago, and I'm sitting in the back of his car, they had half a top. Oh, he had plenty of money. And his chauffeur, my wife, they want to take children. I don't know, they didn't want children. Around the corner from where I'm waiting, I get in the most beautiful apartment, and the man who wanted it was in all this. This is one of the big theaters. And he had a little girl. And he went right fire with my little girl. But she did say, I want to see your daughter. And when I saw her daughter, that was a wildcat. But my daughter was with behavior. Everything worked that way. Their daughter ate in my house, in my apartment all the time. So Issa Jones wants to see me. Then Paul Beesey. You ever hear of Paul Beesey? I've heard the name, but I don't remember if I ever had any hearing. He was a stout man. They operated on him. He took 60 pounds off his stomach and he died. Like that. When he sat at the table for two, he needed to the table for two. The guys in the band said to me, look who's listening to you. I said, you listen to me? He's listening to you. Maurice Sherman, after his leader at the Sher... Marlin, this leader in the Sherman house. He said, I think his name was Sherman. He was a Marlinist. We had a conglomerate mess. We didn't have any band. We had one incident of each. Piano, violin, tenor saxophone, trumpet, trombone, and drums. And the drummer was Victor Burton who wrote the Sob and Blues. You know the Sob and Blues? Oh yeah.
I know him from his records with Nichols and the Wolverines.
Well, his name is Vic Cohen, if you want to know his name.
I know his little brother. I didn't know that was his name.

Burton was his grandfather's name. But she called him at the time, he did seem to like Jews. So he had his name changed to Victor Burton. And incidentally, he got with Alfred Newman, the second drummer, and my brother. And when he found out that my brother was Paul G. D. D. D. D. D. D. D., they were buddy-buddy. I mean his job was secure. You know how he clicked together. The first week I went out to Los Angeles, I must have had dinner in a hundred musicians' houses. They all take me to get acquainted. It's a clique. And it's good to be in the clique. And even if they don't know you, they say they do. I remember Frank Segrest, one of the finest drummers. Have you ever heard of him? Yeah. He didn't know me. He didn't know me. But I knew Segrest's reputation. He knew of my reputation. And when I went out to the Chinese theater with my brother, my brother was playing the Footlight Parade, Jimmy Cagney, just a presentation. Just a, did very little orchestra, played the music, and they did something on the stage. But I'm stuck in a Waterville theater, and I said, if I'm going back to Waterville, I'm going back to New Orleans. But I go up there, and there's San Frank Segrest, he sees Paul, and there comes Johnny. He picks me up, and Johnny, my boy, and he swings me along, and I'm his loving pal, going on a man for a matter. I said, Paul, who is the guy? He's a Segrest. Oh, I said, well, I'm out of him. But that's the way it is. Today, even in this building, they say, you know Johnny Detroit. They don't say, this is Mr. Detroit, because the people might not know me. And I don't know them. And how I find out their name, I ask them their apartment number. Then I go look on the ball. Because they said that they dance to my music when they're young. And they're mostly widows, too, to talk. So, you know Sam, you know Joe, Joe, who, what, Joe, I don't know. So I go look. But it's one of those things. To be a, what would you say, a semi-celebrity, a has-been. The only thing I gratified myself is that I, it's better to be a has-been than I never was. And I'm still, I meet lots of people. And now here's the strange thing, I never blew a note on Bourbon Street in my life. Never blew a note on Bourbon Street. Congratulations. You betcha, I congratulate myself too, aren't ya? But there's a fine band in that, your father's mustache. I want to tell you that. Have you heard him lately? Who is that?
I don't know.
I know that this old-timer that played the clanner with everybody and his brother, he can't read much. Raymond Burke.
Yeah.

Well, you might say he's the weakest man in the band. But they have a colored trumpet player, he gets my vote. Alvin Alcorn. What's his name? Alvin Alcorn. You could tell him I like his trumpet player.
I will, next time I go there.

And you tell the trombone player he's got plenty of power, which is a little too much. He knocked me out of the window. But he plays, brother, he plays. And when you play with that assertion, you can, don't you like these trombone players? Oh, yeah.
That's Jimmy Hayslip, I think.

I don't visit those places, but I'm a lonely, I'm a lonely man, see? And I've been eating at Holmes' cafeteria because I can drive my car up in there and if I stay more than an hour, I don't have to pay any money. Otherwise, I'll have to go all over the district for a place to park and when I get in my car, somebody will hit me on the head and around me, you know? So, I don't find a food man. I can eat. I eat in the Pontchartrain too. But when they charge you a dollar and eighty cents for an armlet, that's time to stop. And not only that, they're sitting in your lap and looking down your throat and everybody... I ate breakfast there one morning, my daughter knew it at noon, your daddy was in the Pontchartrain school. Who's looking at me? But I don't care, my life is an open book. But I do walk down Weber Street because it's amusing. It's nothing but a corny island now. It's not New Orleans. It's changed, but let's have it that way. Sinister is the biggest Barnum and Bailey Shore I ever saw in my life. I go in there and walk over there. All of our boys know me. I've arranged to take a lady to breakfast in that green garden room there. They only serve meals for certain hours, you know? And then I take my daughter and when they come in, they're like, where are you going? Because they like new places. I don't blame them. If you can afford them, let's have them, huh? Like when I went to Miami and said, you want to have a room with your meals? I said, no, sir. Every meal is going to be in a different joint because Miami Beach has more fine restaurants than any place in the world. And don't they feed you? You can gain ten pounds. That stone crab. Huh? That stone crab they have there. Yeah, you bet. The first morning I go in, you see friends of mine say, don't forget to go to Wolf's Don't forget to go to Wolf's. Don't forget to go to Juniors. Don't forget to go to Lush Owls. Don't forget to go. So we go on, let's try a wall. I walk my poor wife about fifteen blocks down to Wolf's and they have a line for singles,
double, quartets.

I mean that's the kind of business to do. I sit down and the waitress comes up and she's at the map of Israel all over her face. She's out for the money. It all hustles. Everybody hustles. So I said, honey, what do you have for breakfast? She said, you order. How about? I said, bacon and eggs, juice, and toast. She says, toast, toast as if it was poison. Where do you see what I'm going to bring here? She said, bring me a basket of every kind of bread. You can make a meal on the bread. The bread was better than the other food. Oh, you know how they do it. Stuff with dates or stuff with garlic or you never know what you're going to hit. Onion, but it's good. The place I liked was Juniors because the tables were far apart. You could go in there, you could voice.
You ever been to Juniors in Miami Beach?
And it might be two bits higher, twenty-fifths of the island, but it's worth ten dollars. You know what I mean? You're on a vacation. You're not going to come down.

You reminded me of something. You talked about getting hit on the head in the district or something. What was the Tango Belt? I'm always hearing people talk about the Tango Belt. Do you know what that was?
I couldn't tell you with any authenticity because I'm only talking about what I know.
You didn't play in that area.

No, I will say this. The Charlie Rittner, who was the first white man in this town to slap a bass, used to call it slapping a bass, you know. Wilbur Dinkle, who was known as the Albinaud of the South. Albinaud in our day was the leading jazz piano player. You never heard of Albinaud. There was a million Albinauds in the United States.
Yeah.

My brother Paul played the drums and I had the trumpet. And we visited all the joints of the district. We played with the Negro bands. I could buy them a little shell of beer for a nickel apiece and I was always welcome, John, because they liked the way I played. And it didn't hurt me. I listened to them play, they listened to me. They didn't play my way, but nobody threw us out. And he'd slap that bass and my brother would beat hell out the drums and we'd have a hell of a little bit of a time. And I was welcome. That's how I met Mr. Robichill, Professor Robichill. You ever hear of him? Yeah. Left-handed violinist. You didn't know that, eh?
We had his orchestration.

Well he was the one with the music of Panama that I recorded. It was written as a Spanish tune. You play it. And we go boom, you know, and you'll put the old swing to it. Yeah. He says I'll let it to you but to no one else. Then there was AJ P. Rohn. You heard of him?
Yeah.

He had the orchestra at Tranchinas, which was competitive to mine, and also the halfway house. There was Tranchinas, the halfway house where the Brunus boys played, and Carl's. And we've got all the business. So there's a lot of people that are traditionals here in New Orleans that I never heard play. I offered a reward to hear a certain, anybody could ever find, find anybody that heard a certain trumpet player but never did find him. But still he's supposed to be great. Where did he play? Where was I when he was playing? Not that I didn't care. I played my way. Like the motorist called me Connie. Why does he care? Huh?
I guess some of those trumpet players went to Chicago very young or something.

Johnny Baisnautha died lately. Did you know that? Yes. Now there was my idea of a Dixieland trumpet. Yeah. Clean as a pen, every note, and a fine style. And I think of all the recordings that O.K. made here that Johnny Baisnautha made the best. That's my idea.
I like that very much. I like him too. Johnny? Yes.
Very modest man. He worked for the commodity something, I don't know.
He didn't get his due.
No. Not at all.
Well that record is known the world over whether the people here recognize it or not now.
I like his playing and I like the impression of him. Yeah. We used to get together and chat because we speak the same language.
Well he was a regular guy.

Oh, listen, musicians, there's a rule of regulars. Take it from me. I know my band, I can show you pictures where they're laughing and they're jolly and they all love one another. And they love their leader in spite of what people think. But they used to try to put me on in lots of ways. I remember I used to, as I tell you, I would take anything to make money and keep them busy. Because my bass player, I had a great bass player named Dan LeBlanc, he died prematurely. He told me one night we would play with you because you get to work. And I said, isn't there any sentiment attached to you guys? Don't you feel that I'm a good guy and that you could depend on me to get you out of jail?
You know?
I had the greatest musicians in this world in my band. I mean in this world. Now that's taken a lot of territory. I had Arthur Ponce, guitarist. Do you know him?
Yes, I know him.
Did you ever have him play?
Yes.
Was he solo?
As near as I could tell. He called me the other night. He said, Dad. Oh, loud too.

He said, you were thinking of me. I said, how do you know? He said, ESP. I said, ESP, you're drunk. Just like that. Me! Screaming. Then he goes on. And I've got to listen to his war record again. Concussion in the brain. He missed nine jobs and I took it. You're drunk, just like that. Me, screaming. Then he goes on, and I've gotta listen to his war record again. Concussion in the brain. He missed nine jobs, and I took it. But one night, he went off on intermission, didn't come back. I found out he was in jail, got in an automobile accident. We rushed down to Poland Street, we get him out of jail, and we get him out. He says to the death sergeant, he says to him, give me my so-and-so money back, and all you so-and-so, you know? Sergeant says, put him back in the clink. I started to say something, he says, you say anything, I'll put you back in the clink. Oh, I'll let him get out of there quickly, they'll put me in jail. So I let him go. I had to let him go. But I'll tell you that I used him on impossible combinations, because I loved his guitar playing. And when I had a bank with a big, something where it didn't require too much loud music, people could hear it, I would ask Arthur to play a couple of his arrangements, like the world is waiting for the sunrise, and I never heard such chords in my heart. I personally was thrilled to that man's playing. So I know, if they didn't know he was good, they'd just hear you. And he's good today, but his father dropped in his arms a couple of weeks ago, and now they're fixing up the estate and somebody's going to grab a hold of that boy. He's about four feet tall and four feet wide. He's a crack shot with a pistol. And when I used to go fishing, he always carried it up there, I figured they'd shoot me. We used to go fishing together. I powered all my, Bob Yeo, afterwards I put him in the union at 16, he's a builder, but he loves to play music. I believe he played for nothing. I mean, he's, Ernest just told me they're playing a job out of town and Bob's on the job, and I know Bob doesn't need the money. I fish with Bob Young. He's the one that I sent to Dr. Brown because he's nauseated every night. That's wrong, he doesn't get enough sleep. But he always was a nervous rink, and always too thin. But such a splendid gentleman. Such a nice wife, nice family. I love my boys. My band periodically, we'd go down on Neanderth Street, there was a place that we called Maceres, and we'd have a, we'd take some of the performers that we liked, and we'd have a spaghetti supper. And we'd have spaghetti and meatballs and some dago red. And we'd get a room upstairs, you know. Comes at about 40 cents a head. Yeah, I'm like, and Perretti, Perretti could eat a platter full of spaghetti. Perretti was a great guy. He had a lot of rock hands. But he played with me at the Liberty. You see, I took him, any time I could get him, I'd take him. So when I went over to the Liberty to take Max Fink's place, he got some scandal. And I was on, you know, as you say, I was on the staff, I was sure of a job. I directed the orchestra to St. Charles when they had dramatic stop. All I did was play between the acts. So all I had to do was head out to dance books. You could play what you played last night. You know, I'd never have nothing to worry about. And played a curtain up. I knew about enough to play a little thing. Well, the curtain went up, you know. Or if it was rain, or something like the African cannibals, I'd go, da da da da da da, boom, jeep, boom. Great. I was the only one who could think of it, because I had played. I always took Perretti around it. He had bad habits. He'd make a bet of two dollars every intermission, which resulted that at the end of the week he lost more than he made. Couldn't stay away from betting. He said, I'm only betting two bucks. I said, but two bets four times a day is eight dollars a day. You're making forty-four dollars a week. That's all he was getting. That was good money in those days. I bet you. Well, I said, why don't worry about that? It doesn't affect his climate plan. He's actually going to play in my own business. But then I had to put on an overture every week. And Max Fink, when he left there, was playing poet and peasant. Overture. I think he did it to put me on, because I'm the man on the box now. I'm the man with the trumpet. I'm leading the orchestra with the trumpet. And Elmore Ryan, the manager, said, what are you going to play, Johnny? He's playing poet and peasant. I said, I'm going to play poet and peasant.
He says, are you not a trumpet?

I said, I know it backwards. I stood up and played the whole overture from beginning to end, and when I got to the finish, I took it as a tactical, and the house come down there, and I never heard a trumpet player play the poet and peasant over to you on the trumpet. So that's the way you put yourself over. I made the only decent broadcast, the first decent broadcast in the city of New Orleans. When I was at Liberty, I was playing the Full Horseman from the Apocalypse. And I had Madame Guipaul, who was a leading sopranauty opera at the time. I had her that week to sing the Marseilliers, you know, for the overture, and then we'd go into the picture with Rudolph Valentino. So they asked me to come up and broadcast, which is something new to me. I never did that broadcast. And I had thirteen men, and I played Raymond Overture. I went and described it fine in the papers. It said the thunderous tones of Raymond Overture. You know, it opens up, . We played it all week. We could play with the eyes closed. It was duck soup. I enjoyed myself. They heard us as far as Napoleon Avenue. I didn't know.

You didn't get that. I didn't know it was duck soup though. I thought it was Ron Sophie. Did you hear what I said in the last one, won't you go? Yeah, I know. You go. Yeah. We get the wires kept coming in. You're coming in clear. Napoleon to St. Charles. Oh, I loved it. I have the write-ups there. Take me. It was a swell.
It was a swell.
It was a swell.
It was a swell. It was a swell. It was a swell. It was a swell.
It was a swell.
It was a swell. It was a swell. It was a swell. It takes you a long time to read them. We don't have time for that.
Oh, I wanted to ask you.
Ask me something that you want to know.
Yeah, that I want to know too. Your band sounded different in the New York recording from the New Orleans recording. It is, huh? And I was wondering why.

Maybe they went and got some good New York musicians to put them in there. I didn't know that. They'd feel that all over the world. Don't you know that my brother went to the studios? If you can't hit a high note, they'll have one to hit it for you. If you can't sing the high note, they got somebody who can sing it. They'll dub anything. They'll dub anything. A case of point was that Alfredo and the musicians never see the picture they're recording for. Did you know that?
No, I didn't.

They wouldn't go see it if you gave them a ticket. They just play the music. And in the drum section, it's done electrically, like the leader. They have earphones because of everything. So they do, they have arranges. Guys say, give me 12 minutes or 12 seconds of a guy falling off a cliff or a horse or something. They jot it down. It'll last again. Nip it off. Join it together. All spells mother. Band never sees the picture. It's all timed.
But your New York recordings had a two-bone. They're too long you say? No, there's a tuba, tuba player.

I had a tuba player, Barney Aquilino. He was with James Barney. I got him afterwards in New York. And he was more or less my promoter. He got me in the middle of a dance hall. I wore up in Harrisburg, Pennsylvania. There was two dance halls, big ball, beautiful big ball. They were fighting each other. And I happened to play at the six day bicycle races. You see I lived a long life, and I'll tell you a long, I mean a musical life. I'm playing at the six day bicycle races for the benefit of poor children. And in the box there there's Vincent Lopez and God knows who, all the big mansees and all. They offer a hundred dollars for a sprint. Well if I say, who wins that sprint, it gets a hundred bucks. And the sprint's all night. So they asked me to play. I said certainly for poor children. I go there with my band. They don't have a piano. Well we've got to play. So I played It Had To Be You. And they had an arrangement in stop time where I took all the breaks. The band goes, It had to be you. And I come in, all over the joint. You know like that way. Crap. But good. You know. They're all up there, who is this guy? So they said, no, Johnny D. Dre from the Halls, I play another tune. Every prize fighter and bum from the Halls that was in New York was on my bandstand looking for a handout. And I'm playing for nothing in the joint, see. But the next morning, my phone rings incessantly. I'm off and jump. Everybody wants to be my agent. Everybody wants to be my agent. So I signed up with Vincent Lopez. And he appointed Mrs. Marvin Fuller, Mrs. Earl Fuller as my manager. You never heard of Earl Fuller? Carman Blair? No. Band leader from the Pacific Coast. When he made his entrance to New York, he was on special train. He recorded for Victor, didn't he? I think he did. I don't know. But anyhow, his wife, he died and his wife became an agent. And she sends me to Harrisburg. She goes to Oakland to You know what I mean? In those days. So I paid the boys' hotel booth. I could have stuck it in my pocket. They didn't know what I was getting. Because I had them on the contract for $75 a week. And $25 for each recording. That's all they got for the recording. But I got a lump sum on it. $50 and 2% royalties. So Vincent Lopez is the only one who sent me a while when I opened this to Burbank. I put it in my scrapbook. I wish you had success in a long engagement. I mean he's a man that does things. He's getting old now. He still plays Nola and all that. Last time I saw him he didn't know I was in the place. I didn't want to impose myself on him. I think they have to entertain him. And my wife and I only had two weeks. We saw 13 shows in 11 days. And I'd get the tickets. Don't think I didn't. See Ray Bowles is a personal friend of mine. I played golf with Ray in his show. He was being featured. I'm talking about this a long time ago. And then for Oklahoma and Carousel and all I'd go up and give the... After everybody was seated inside the show I'd talk to the man at the box office and I'd say, this is my card. I'm an auctioneer from New Orleans. I'm on a bus and it's holiday. And if you've got two seats any day, any matinee, I'll take it. And I always got seats without pants. I saw the original version of Show Boop, Charlie Whittaker. I knew Charlie Whittaker. He was married to Blanche Franey. You ever heard of Blanche Franey?
She was in early movies, in silent movies?

When I was a youngster, before I was married. And Charlie played a little clarinet. In fact, he gave me the clarinet and I sold it. I sold it for $15. He says, who wants a clarinet? I said, I'll take it. He was trying to play the clarinet. But anybody that's like Jack Benny. Jack Benny always was down in the pit with us. I mean, down in the cellar. And we used to joke because he went on after the dogs. And he says to me, don't you think they ought to sweep the stage before I come on? We got to be friends. We didn't know that was to be the great... Like when I met Al Joltzl. Well, when Al Joltzl asked me if I could play for him, the way I was playing, the way I was playing in the pit, I mean with the orchestra, he meant fill up the long, so he wouldn't have to hold those long notes, I'd have to fill them up. They're what they call, make the breaks. I said, Sightly. He said, well you're the boy I want. When I sing, you play. Don't play for anybody else. And that meant a victory of a contract. And the day I'm sitting in the box at the palace, which was the White House of Lauderville in those days, in the old days, Lucia, better known as Frisco, the Zillophon, he comes up to the box and says, Dad, we're going to start recording tomorrow. I said I'm awful sorry, I'm going home.
Frisco, the guy who wrote Check It and Break It?

No, he had a Spanish name that wasn't too good for the stage, they called him Frisco. But it was a great telephone. He recorded for Edison, Edison didn't last long, but it was a contract. I recorded with Johnson from Brunswick, you never know I'm in it, but I'm playing.
I've seen some of those recordings with Johnson. Did you solo with him? Can you hear yourself on him? No.

No. We had another fellow from the Russian Symphony, Eisenhower. He played lead trumpet and I played hop trumpet. But I will say that I created more attention than he did because I get up and take a chorus and it was absolutely strange to their ears. I toured the, they offered the theater clothes with an act called Adelaide Hughes. I don't know whether you remember that. They were two of the greatest dancers that ever lived. She was known as La Petite Adelaide. He danced on her toes. And Jimmy Hughes was an athletic sort of a dancer. He did an Indian dance and I swear he leaped the queen across the stage. So their violinist was drafted. They had no leader. But they had a spot in their show where they had to have something happen because it was a two act and they had to change their clothes for the finale. And Mr. Tasso played a miserable violin. He directed well, but when he tried to play something it wouldn't do to kill the spot. So they heard me playing down in the pit and they came to me and said, will you go with us on the interstate second? I said, well I'll talk to my wife. She said, how long is it? She said, it's six weeks. And she said, never one of those unnecessary jobs, you know what I mean? But she wouldn't, she knew I was ambitious, she knew how musicians were so. She said, we want you for one reason. In the middle of our act, as you know, instead of the violinist, we want you to fill that spot. I said, I can do it. It's probably me anyway. So I made a, I grabbed a hold of two stock orchestrations. One was the sunshine of your smile. You remember that?
Yes.

And I, I hooked that onto the storybook ball for no reason whatsoever except that I had an orchestration that I could waste all the storybook ball. I would paste them up. And then I hadn't reached that stage where I had the radius done. So I pasted them together and wrote in a modulation. And I'd stand up and, wait.
And attached to it was the chorus of some of these days.
Attached to Storybook, though?

Yes, sir. They used to send out the orchestrations with two pieces, just like you say, a platter, with the flaps, what do you call it, the flap? What's the side they don't expect? The flip side. The flip side. They give you two pieces, one orchestration. So I put that on there. So if I went big, and I always went big, not to brag, I'd get up and I'd give them those three-fifths notes, and we'd go into it, knock them stiff. Easy. Easy. But maybe luck. Maybe just do good judgment. Maybe some inborn experience. I told this one, because Texas hadn't heard any jazz. The leader at the Rice Hotel, I knew him very well, his name was Finley. And the bassist was the same fella that I told you was the first man ever to... They invited me to play a night on the rice roof. The Rice Hotel was the center of Houston's nightlife. Well, the trumpet player, he got disgusted, I guess, and he thought he was outside, he went home and left me stuck with the job for the night. So I stayed there and played, and Finley asked me if his name was... Could I get plenty to join with me and come join his orchestra? Tony and I were doing something, you know, fairly, you know, didn't want to go. So this trumpet player said, Johnny, I want to thank you for filling out the night for me, I want to give you something. And he has me a can of metal polish. I had a brass trumpet at that time because, you know, I thought I could get a better tone out of it, and all I ever polished was the bell, because that's all the people could see. It was a miserable looking horn, but it was a great horn, I'm telling you, it was like another painted Stradivarius, it had it, you know what I mean?
Yeah.

He insults me, gives me a can of metal polish. I said, well, I'll remember you, Mr. Miller, Mr. Arthur Miller. Just jealous, that's all. And everywhere I went, the bands were being depleted by the war, the best men were being tricked, drafted, and the leaders were taking jobs as bandmasters and all that stuff. It was a good thing they brought me along, because I was the one who would set the tempo, not the drummer, the strange drummer. I'd give them that, I'd play a waltz, I'd give them that, with the trumpet, not making three notes, it'd be so decisive that they were glad they had me. But I got the fluids, I lost ten pounds. I tried to stand up and play solos with the flu, but I showed up and I played, so I banged off every four weeks. When I got off the train, my wife didn't know me. I looked so bad. It was nice to know Adelaide News, and they loved me and all like that, they loved my player. And the show traveled as a unit, I got to know all the people on the show, they were all nice friends, you know. It was called the Interstate Center. I did a lot of things, like Mr. Cobb, when they started putting acts in, Mr. Cobb didn't know one act from the other, he didn't want to spend any money. And those were playing split weeks. You know what they call split weeks? Three days and then four days. Well I get the acts that were laying off. I had to build posters for $25 a piece and all they could eat. Carl's restaurant. Guy says, I spent more than $25 on the car. I said, you get it for nothing, sign the check, and $25. A hundred dollars they call. And he said, well we're going to do two songs. I said, yeah, you're going to do a dozen if they clap, because I know they're all hams, they're all one of them. They like you enough, they get on that floor and do it for 45 minutes. That's all they sure I needed. I had the tops. I got Mary Riley. I don't know whether I heard them, but she was another Bee Palmer. The Orient would bring in Bee Palmer, I'd have to go dig up another cool shower somewhere, so I'd dig them up out of loads or somewhere and get them for the split weeks. And Mr. Cobb loved me, and he should. Don't you think? Well he has. He has the highest 550 people a night. That's past history. I can prove it, but it's facts. And I get in my share. I was the only man he ever gave a Christmas present to. He gave me a hundred dollars and almost dropped in. And he had, another thing, he did give presents to the busboys. He employed only deaf-mutes as busboys. He was a kind man, he was a fine man. And I go to his farm, he had a beautiful farm out on old Gentile Road, you ever hear of it? Next to Robert Hall. They own all that Robert Hall. In fact, Mrs. Cobb died and left a couple of million dollars to her family. And I could have married one of her nieces. But she was fresh from Germany. Boy she was socks to hog her if you ever saw one. She had Germany written all over her face. She had nothing. But there was a wonderful family. I was sitting home on Broadway in St. Charles, a beautiful house. He had a ratzkeller with a piano, he loved music. And when I played the dealer session, I always had to play some German music. Because you got all the German captains and mates from the ships and all that coming in. And I bring them back to Germany a little bit. And one day he said to me, what are you doing with your money? I said, that's better. I'll send you a subdivision, he says, from golf ports. All built up for $15,000. I hold some. I said, why? He said, I don't want to be bothered. I said, if I owe this man $15,000, I got to be a lifetime job in this place. You know what I mean? But I didn't see any further than this. I didn't buy it. You're musicians. You're a musician. You're nothing else. Nothing else. You're a musician. You live and die. You're making arrangements and trying to improve the other guy who's better than you to start off with. You're trying to arrange them. Now my idea, I write this with the long record. It's the best, if you call it Dixieland, jazz still written, is South Ramport Street Parade. Every straight in that thing is a different idea. Did you notice that? And it was written by two fellas, Bob Haggard the bass player and Raymond Baduk the drummer who couldn't read a note as big as the Custom House. But maybe Raymond could whistle him.
Yeah.

Raymond used to sub, if my brother had a late show, I was making so much money I quit the office. It wasn't interesting anymore. You know I'm a leader. Because I had an outfit in Morrison's cafeteria. He used to have music there. I have outfits all over. And so if the off you had a late show, Raymond was playing at some cheap joint on Bourbon Street but he'd take his intermission at that time so he could rush in and open them with us at Cobb's. And my brother would give him a couple of dollars. And he was supposed to be one of the greatest sticks of my drummers. I couldn't see him. Because he used to juggle the sticks too much. My brother was down, you know. That Moncais style. That's another good drummer.
Moncais.

I used him, I couldn't keep him because he drank too much. I had to have respectable, he had no teeth. Well you're going to have some tape recording there. Well everybody would sell that. Well I want to tell you, it's a big deal.
Monk would sell that himself. Let me get you a bit.
All right. Fine. And some day when you have nothing to do it would take 24 hours. All right. Now I have an ice box that I have to get in the hall to open.
You want anything to eat? Oh, just a Pepsi would fix me. All right. You want a little beer? You want some wine?
I have some better chips.
Pepsis are fine for us. Huh? Pepsis are fine for us. We both like Pepsi. Just like this. No ice in it. Just like that. Just like that. Right on the bottle. I know. I guess you can't.
You know I did stuff myself. You know. I would take that night. You know. It's time to make you sleep. Instead of somenics. Brother this is something. I'm keeping house. Can you imagine that?
Well. We all have to learn.
The bathroom is right back there if you want to go. I'm right. You know. I'm right. I'm right.
I'm right. I'm right. I'm right.
I'm right. I'm right. I'm right.
I'm right.
I'm right. I'm right. I'm right. You're good. No.
You never know. No. I took a lady to dinner one night.

Recently because you see my wife had been dead for three months. You can't live alone. And she said, John, I'm going to the girls room. And I said to myself, thank God. But she said that her first husband had told her, whenever we go out and we get, when we pay the check, please go to the girls room so I can go to the men's room. Thank you. Well, I mean, I mean, nice people. This lady is highly educated. She makes me watch my piece and cue this. But she doesn't care about that. She doesn't produce it. And I, she's such a wonderful company. Wonderful. Okay. Not because she doesn't build me up. Of course, when you introduce me to somebody and I want a pedestal, I'm going to fall off and crack my neck. I'm going to drink a Pepsi with you. Do you know why? Right ahead. I made my breakfast the other morning. I made my breakfast. And after I cleaned the frying pan, I said, never again. For 80 cents, I can get everything from soup to nuts, down at the crystal. I'm going to drink a Pepsi with you. Do you know why? Right ahead. I have eggs and bacon and cheese. I made my breakfast the other morning. I made my breakfast. And after I cleaned the frying pan, I said, never again. For 80 cents, I can get everything from soup to nuts, down at the crystal. And for now, in 80 cents, I can get an arm like that. That's right. You want to go ask? I didn't offer you a glass. No, this is fine. This is fine. What do you think about it? You think I'm full of bone?
No, this is fascinating. This is great stuff.
What I'm telling you is actually facts, not colored. I can tell you some things that knock you cold. If the lady wasn't present, I'd tell them to keep it up. Well, we're cold, ain't you?
No, I'm not going to speak.
Anyhow, it's best to appear, gentlemen.
But this is interesting. You've brought up your names.

Oh, I wouldn't want to. I wouldn't know. A musician is bound to have strange experiences. I played places I was afraid to go in. For instance, the man in Miami from Charmpton Beach, which is Patterson, Louisiana. You heard of him? Are you available? Yes. Some of you are particular. I demand a deposit. I drive up to the place, I say, it can't be possible. But after they turn the lights on and all the society people come in there, it's a beautiful place. They've got a good band and a good crowd. It's the same as the auditorium under Roosevelt. It's no different. But it's an unpainted building and you're afraid you say, well, I played in Picayune one night in the dead of winter. They didn't have a windowpane in the windows. They were all broken off and the kids, and the guy had to go screw fuses in before we could get some lights. And I said to the man in the oil station, where is this dance being held? He said, down, a little piece down the road. I said, this must be it. And I'll look in there. And gee, some of the flooring was down and some was up. But I had been engaged by the postmaster, who was a man of integrity. I didn't have to work. I'm telling you, we were all waiting in the dark until they screwed the fuses in. Oh, I played places where we couldn't use the piano. We turned the back of the piano to the audience, they never knew whether we were a pianist or not. He didn't play it. I told him, don't you dare touch it all on a tune. I played one time at the Arabian High School. They wrote the piano around. It was white. They had used it for chicken roots. It was white. But I happened to have Frank Curety with me then as a pianist who was a very fine, legitimate piano player. I had good rhythm. Frank, I love Frank. We used to. But he loved bolts and motors and he'd come with his fingernails full of grime. So I said, there's only one thing we can do, Frank, is cut your nails down to the quick and scrub it with some lava soap or something like that. Because he'd forget about the job and come be working on his motor. And then people look at him, he'd be in the stands, especially if he's a good one, you know? So Frank says, what will I do? I said, well let's see if we can use it. If it's too much out of tune, I'd throw it out. I wasn't going to have my saxophones all out of tune. I'd rather have one piano out than have nine men all out of tune. And Frank used to carry a tuning hammer with him. Oh, he was the piano player you'd have. Because when we used to play in the patio room, the moment we walk in, the manager sent up a red tray or drink. Why? Because you're going to get a free piano tuning job from CUNY.
