Because one day we went and the pedals were all on the bumper. CUNY was under the piano, Martin was sitting at the piano trying to fix the pedals. And he wanted to do a job, you know? Well that's a conscientious person, isn't it? So he carried a tuning hammer. And when we get, he tuned the middle register. So I guess the next piano player, when he started to go down up high or down low, he found out he was about a quarter of a tone out from the middle register. But Frank would stay in the middle register and wouldn't devote too much time to the bass because we had a bass. Let the bass man play the right bass notes, you know? I mean he wouldn't reach down. He'd play the phantom bass. They call that a phantom bass. They don't hit anything. It's just moving the hand. Nobody thinks he's playing. He can hit the damn thing. I remember one night, I used to play at the Gulf Coast Military Academy. It's a school for boys, a preparatory school. You've heard of it, haven't you?
Yeah.

They liked me because I treated professors with respect and I acted like a professor. I didn't act like a jazz musician, you know what I mean? And I always got the job. That at Gulf Paul College. That's a good school. And we drive up there and I want to get there at least 45 minutes, half hour at a time. Couldn't get in. I have to wait until the professor come open the door and lock the door. Because they didn't want the kids to be inside. Same way at Ursula and Carmen. We drive up. It's no use to come on ahead of time at Ursula and Carmen. You had to wait until the sister come and lock the door. Up there the sisters handle the scenery, turn on the lights and do everything. I played up there many times. They liked me. I was a gentleman. And they all sit in a row and they looked like a lot of penguins. And I'd play I Believe. You know I Believe? Oh, he's religious. I believe. And Al Black would get up and say it in his unsatan baritone. No, I love Al. I took Al. I was living in Lakeview and a handsome young man comes and knocks on the door and he's called and he says, man, can I get you interested? And a floral lamp. I guess you wonder what that tall lamp did. But you know why I got that thing? So I can read my paper. I have to have my paper with my coffee or I'm miserable. So this young man knocks me out and I come to the door. He didn't know that but the night before I had been out of the suburban going to scowlting the band. I wanted to scowl Ponds off of Ponds. I wasn't a scholar of Al Blanco. I had heard that Pons was good. I said, do you want a guitar? Get the Pons. So I got there and I talked to him back, I didn't let anybody know I was in a joint, and they did a jam session. Red Mackie had the band, I believe. You heard of Red Mackie.
Yes, I didn't.

Natural born musician, but he didn't need it. People had money. And they had a jam session. And I had a chance to get a load of Blanco and Pons. And I was delighted. So I said, Blanco, do you know who I am? He says, I believe you're Johnny DeGroote. I said, I am. He said, Mr. DeGroote, I'm so happy to meet you. I said, I don't need a lamp. I said, but I do need a trumpet player. Will you play with me? He almost fainted. I can't. I don't raise your bed. I said, that's for me to judge. So I took him on. And he come on and down with a little bit of bass and trumpet. It's one of the finest made, but cornet. And the week after that we had the Donaldsonville Fair. I brought to the band. We had caps on. We had caps on. We had white suits with black ties. But you know, in the military. I had a fellow on Ramport Street make me some caps. And I played the, all we had to play was the Overture. And Urie Long was in power then. So naturally it was every man a king. We played chorus of every man a king. That was the Overture. Easiest Overture I ever got by. I had a fellow from his name was Hickey from years ago. I don't know, he used to call us, ha ha ha, Hickey, on the radio. He acted as I.M.C. and he'd introduce me with a lot of flowery words and what would I play? I would call us a, but I played the show like they had never had it played before. We had the Blondin' Realms from Pornham and Bailey Six, German, we had acrobats. And of course they were out in the field and we were up in the grandstand. So knowing they were German I played Under the Double Eagle March. I had my books full of stuff because I never knew what I was going to run into. And they'd come out and they'd be boom, oh, they'd straighten up like Germans. And they'd watch them and when they'd start to pull them stuff I'd go up into a Strauss Balls. Those fellas want to kiss me. I said, well they're recording, you're going to have it, they haven't recorded. Give it to the next man, tell them the player don't record it. And then I'd take them down and when they'd come down to the bar, I'd play a gallop while they'd slide them down. You know you've got to wait until they'd come down one at a time. I'd play a gallop and when they'd face the audience I'd give them a big chord and I'd march them off to boom, boom, boom, boom. Oh boy, they'd wish they could carry me around. I said this is far enough. The job was so easy that we could come home every night if it felt like it. I'd get the quarter of the night fair. But I enjoyed it.
I wanted to ask you one thing before I forget it. Did you take any choruses with Arnold Johnson on the records?

No, never. Just ensemble. Just ensemble. Well he was a piano leader and he featured himself. And the only time I would get a good crack at it was when he would leave the bandstand like in Hamilton, Ontario. He'd go off with the committee and have drinks or something. Then the first trumpet player would double on piano. And I'd take over. I'd leave the band. I'd play pop tunes. The tunes of the band were like down home in Tennessee and all that kind of stuff. Because they didn't know any addiction to it. But I always found a spot where I could live a little bit, you know. I remember we had to go back on the bandstand that night. We got off the bandstand without playing God Save the Queen. And we were off the bandstand packing up. And they come back there and I was like, Mr. Johnson you didn't play God Save the Queen. Well Johnson says, why? He says, well that's the way they close the dances in Hamilton, Ontario. You play God Save the Queen. So we go back on the ball and as we leave in they give us each an imperial quart of whiskey. We went and we got on that train loaded around with booze or something. Imperial quarts, you know those big quarts. I love that little, it was one night, other fellas were sleeping but I got up and I said, I'm going to eat my breakfast in this hotel. It's the last thing. It was the Royal Connaught. It was strictly English. And Hamilton, have you been there?
Never.

It's an English city. The Barbies wear the high hats and the waiters in the restaurant, they got the striped vest. And he comes up to me and he's bowing all over me like he's a mullard somebody. I'm nobody but he's a top player but anyhow. I said, this is an experience for me, mister. You tell me what to eat. I want an English breakfast. He starts me off with fish. Fish for breakfast. I ate it. I ate anything he gave me. And it wasn't costly. I didn't care what it cost. I make 200 bucks a week and I'm not full of money. But that was an experience that I remember. Because I read a lot of English books. I'm not reading as many now. I go for mystery books mostly. Creasy and all the rest of them. And if I was to go to Europe, which I am contemplating, because my wife and I didn't go when we had the chance. You see when I was 45 I contemplated retiring at 45. I had a bankroll. Doctors took it all away from me. So if I go to England, I just want to stay in London, I want to meet all the jazz musicians, some of whom I know, some I don't. I want to hear them play, maybe play with them. And I've been interviewed by writers from France. I mean take my picture standing around, but they insisted on me in a sports shirt. I do not look good in a sports shirt. I'm not the type. I'm used to being fully clothed, you know. And I'm not that type that's looking for cheap publicity. I hate it, and I'm not the same as the other guy, but that's the way I am, you know. So my daughter said, Daddy, your trousers are too wide. I went down and got some, I'm making a, that was my, I don't even have a hi-fi. That was my combination radio, television and record player. So one of my neighbors, Dell, he fools around with that stuff and I told him if you take it all out, I'll give it to you because I want to keep the cabinet. I'm making a liquor cabinet and I don't drink. But I make, but I put books on the other side. I can't go to my books to the library because I can't bring too much. I'm giving stuff away every day. The other day I parked down on the Burgundy Street. I'm going to say it like New Orleans, Burgundy. Some people say Burgundy. I don't know how to say it sometimes. I have a woman, a colored girl in the library telling me how to pronounce my name. I said, Miss, I know how to pronounce my name. I said, I'm pronouncing it the way they do in New Orleans, which is De-Droit. My name is De-Gro. But I'm known as Johnny Detroit. And I'm not going to correct him. Everybody on the Gulf Coast, they're so sweet. They're high class people. Mr. Detroit, I'm going to say my name is, I went so far to put my name in the phone book twice. I'm going to keep it right. That would cause more arguments. You say, I didn't need to write. Why argue over a thing like that? What a little argument.
I could get you on the phone anyway and hire you.
My idea was don't lose that job.
Right.

It might be a friend trying to get me. It might be a friend from out of town who wants to pay me a visit. My phone, as long as my wife was sick, no one knew my phone number. And one of my ex saxophonists who was part of my success came to town and the unionist had phone me first to ask me if I would let them give Rudolph Levy my phone number. I said, sure, give it to Rudolph. So I went to visit him. He stopped at the term mountain. We had chinchin for hours over. I don't know what his wife thought about him. He was his second wife. She's a nice woman too. He teaches bands now. He used to travel for the con company demonstrating the instruments. He was a clever man. The only man ever had to play a tune on a soprano saxophone. That is the B-A-S-T instrument, a soprano saxophone. It's so hard to play in tune on it, see? But he could play anything on tune. Some men are just natural born musicians. Ask me some more, sir. Yeah, about lessons. Who did I take from? Fabian. From Farley and Fabian. And how did he teach you? What did he do? He taught me from the Auburn method, which every trumpet player used, A-R-B-A-N, who was also a graduate and teacher at the Paris Conservatory of Music. My teacher was a first prize pupil from the Paris Conservatory, and he went back to France to help him out in World War I. And he died of something around with his bronchitis. I had bronchitis. They said I had chronic bronchitis just from that night work, playing trumpet, staying out all hours of night. But I'll say this, since I've retired, I don't have any more coughs, terrific coughs. But I used to see, I used to get fireworks displays, I used to suffer, cough, cough, cough, cough, cough. Now I don't, because I don't get up, I run from the wrong two-lane room out into the cold street to go over to the A&G to get a cup of coffee, because they wouldn't make you one, and you know, you're trying to, you know, try a thermos, the thing, but kind of a cheap guy. I never looked for favors anyhow, I never did. I'd go out of my way not to have to ask anything. If I asked a waiter to bring a man out of some ice water, he knew he could give a buck, give him a dollar. You've got to pay your way. And when I go in the blue room I'm a mock man, because they know me. The captain would come up and he'd say what did he do, did he take your order? He wants to give you five. Oh, I'd spend the five. I'd give it to the shoeshine boy. Like this, the suit. I went down to get a piece of some plywood cut to make this thing I'm going to make here. I have to use screws, they don't light a hammer in here, you don't use screws. So I drill a little hole with my drill number. I said to the man, he's an old man, but he's about my size. I said, you want this suit? He said, yeah. I said, well, wait till I get it off. I mean, my daughter says, get rid of it. So I'm the kind of a guy who doesn't like to see anything go to waste. These men who work in this place here tell you. The other day I gave them a thing that you put behind your hair when you wash your hair. I don't know how it got in the back of my car, they must have thrown everything in the back of the car. I gave away fishing tackle. I have plenty, I have too much. I'm a fellow that can't resist fishing tackle at the park. I've got to go in there and get something, buy something. It's a result that I have too much. And I had three bad vices, very bad. I like to fish, hunt and play golf. That's why I don't look 77, that's what they say. I don't know. But Mama lived to be 94. And I heard my lawyer, in the succession, they read something there that they think my lifespan will be 88. I don't know why that's in there, why is that in there? Well, if I left 88, I thank God right now. I'll try to be a good boy the rest of my life. And I have been a good boy.
I'll bet you make it.

I think I will, because I, this lady that I met, and I don't mind telling you I like her very much. She's somebody that I have never met before. I don't know if this is because she's considerate. And I told her the other night, I said, you know, what makes me like you so much? I said, you're just like my mother. Now, I don't know whether I made a hit or not telling her. She might think I'm a mother's boy, which I never was. But my mother was a kindly, considerate person. Everybody loved her. She lived to be 94. And she enjoyed life to the hills. And we have a picture of my daughter's of her, which is, the man that took that picture, he took her character. It's just a wonderful picture of my mother. It's a big one. Now, there's a hunk of nothing that I used to cover up rat holes. When I was moving out, three people wanted to buy it. So I said, yes, I'll sell it. He said, how much? I said, $250. But they didn't buy it. I think it cost six. Here's one. My daughter says, Daddy, you must take that lamp down because it's hiding the picture. I love this picture. I bought this picture at McRory for $3.44. I don't know if it's a single copy of a scene in Venice. Canal in Venice by Chanel. He must have been a great artist. It's one of his copies, you know. And I dirty made a frame a little bit to make it look. My color frame would be good. I think nothing of buying a whole dollars worth of paint to put one center. I spray you, I can't use it, but you see the colors? Look at the light shining back there. And my daughter says she swears she was there. She thinks so now. They had a nice trip. Of course they went on a guided tour. Oh yeah. And she says that's the best way to go because you don't know what to do. You might miss something otherwise. Now you see those two over there? You didn't see those? Of a trumpet? Yeah, I saw them on a trumpet. My brother? I came in. It's supposed to be me. You can barely see it. I knew that.
I knew that the minute I came in.
I saw that the first half. Did you carry that much weight? Were you that heavy? No, I weighed 180 one time. I weighed about 149. Which is right now.
Yeah, you feel better now.

Oh. And the tailor, the man who makes alterations on the clothes, he measured me and said, Hallelujah. Before that, it was a constructive job. I had a prominent aid and a prominent aid, and a pants over here. So now I can walk off with the suit on. And if it's an expensive suit, all I have to do is shorten the sleeves. Because good clothes have more material, you know.
That's another thing.

In my heyday, I wore only Stein Rock. Dobbs hats. I still nut on hats. I pick $18, $20 per hat. Well, you can't get a decent hat. I'm right now debating what hat I'm going to wear with my sport coat. I've got to please my daughter. And this one. This girl, is she on the ball? Oh! Generic of a boy named Frank Downley. He's a wonderful fellow. He's in electronics, not in Houston. Making plenty of money. She threw away 28 shirts more to her dad. Because they were out of style. Well, he can afford them. He has four departments at Crowns. He has four shoe departments at Crowns. If I let her in here, she's going to throw my shirts away, I'll kill her. Because they're not all form-fitting. I have my only arrow shirts on Manhattan. And when I bought all these white shirts, they didn't have them fitted. Yeah. Why should I throw them away? Who sees it? Everybody knew what the name of my shirt was. Is that an Arden? Yeah. All right. If I like Arden, that's my business. I'm paying the five and a half for it. One up a half an hour. And maybe when I go back, it'll be two of them. I used to eat... Don't take this, Don. Please, shut it up. I wouldn't, sir.

And they round dance and they do this, that and the other. I'm not going to interfere in their life. You know what I mean? Look at that stationery, the groom hall. This is a photostatic copy, you know? Now tell me when it starts to talk.
It's okay.

Well, this is a letter from Nick LaRocca, original cornetist with the original Dixieland man. I'm writing to him, I'm at the groom hall. I said, Dear LaRocca, I'm pleased to receive from you a copy of your Blue and the Blues. It is very popular here and I have requests for it every night. No doubt you know I have a jazz band at the groom hall hotel. Barry is again playing with us. We play most of your numbers each night. Tiger Ray, I got Tiger Ray in parentheses. Keep up the good work. Wishing you success and all the other boys who might know me, I am your friend. Your friend John D. Drey. Postscript. Do you remember the blackboard in the excelsior pool room? Where you learned to read music? I taught him to scale on the blackboard in the pool room. I used to take violin lessons from William Spector and Felicity and I had to pass that pool room to go home. And I'd walk home to say the nickel. And he was in there. And I knew he was a rocker. I knew he was trying to play trumpet. I taught him to scale. And he always liked me and he always boosted me. I've been trying to reminisce on an incident and it won't come back to me now that I think it's just the thing that you might be looking for. But I didn't know what you... They come and go. My memory... The filing cabinet is beginning to get weak. That grows up by age I guess, huh? Well...
Well no, but lack of practice. No more to talk to.
You see if I talk to you overnight, you say some word maybe it would bring back some incident.
Alright, what about The Strand? I'll bring back an incident. The Strand...

The Strand was a long picture theater. And it had... Most of the time it had Don Filippini as the director. He could get more out of a waltz and most of them could get out of a symphony. Then afterwards it had Castro Carraza who went over to the singer. But he couldn't play Stardust unless he got the record and found out what the tempo was. He didn't know A from a bull's foot but he could stand up there and direct the orchestra. He was stiff as a post. Mr. Barr used to tell him, Castro get down off that sump box. Get down amongst the people. He would never unbend. And the reason why I was in the singer orchestra was because I had a contract for two years at the St. Charles and they had to close up. They didn't have any air conditioning. So Mr. Garinger who was the general manager and a personal friend of mine, he happened to be in Biloxi on vacation. And he says, Johnny that's a nice band you have there. I said, coming from you Mr. Garinger, I said it's quite a compliment. I said that's the band you ought to have in the pit at the St. Charles. That was dramatic stock. Seven nights and two matinees. Just like five days to play golf and go hunting. And played out the dance books. He says come see me when you come to town. So we closed over there Labor Day. I had come see Mr. Garinger. I got a week off. So I said we might as well cash in on this week off but let's get this contract. He said well I want you for two years. He wanted me. I said you can make it ten. Is that kind of a job? I could get the carbs you know. I used to have to hustle. Easiest job in the world. Played a couple. And after they got the scenery set and the weeks that we only used one set I might not finish a tune before the second act would go on. So it was so easy. And still we couldn't take the job properly because one night we didn't play the people out. Half of the guys were playing pool and the other was the bowling alley. And I don't have any band. I can't find any musicians. Well I let it go but I impressed all of them in the future that that was his job you know. But they didn't need to. So that's the kind of job we had. Now I went into this sign of why. Mr. Garinger said Johnny you're one of the family. I said well you put that in writing. He said well we don't know how long we're going to exist but you are one of the family. You'll always have a job. Being a married man I said well that sounds alright. This job and some others will go together you know. So he said we want you to go into the Sanger. You won't have any responsibility. You're just side man. You're in the band. And we give you $135 a week. Well that was pretty fair money in those days. More than I did. I said $135 a week. He said yeah. I said and the extras. Because we had extras. We got $16 a week extras to play the floor show. Play the stage show. And overtime. So some weeks we had some beauts. I remember one week I took 16 encores on Mason Street Blues. How anybody could stomach 16 choruses by me I don't know it. But every time I stopped the house would come down. Ben Black would sing. And Ben Black he was the master's son. I'd be playing Just the Memory. And he'd be saying to the audience isn't that beautiful. Listen to that boy. I'd play Just the Memory you know. I'd play Day is Done. Copy. Copy. And he'd be staring up there with his bat horns. Idolizing old Johnny you know. You can't mess with an MC. And he says I want to tell you fellas something. I'm easy. I don't know at all. I'm only a banjo player. But he had good jobs. He tried to get me to go to Barron Longs and join him in San Francisco. Long before he ever saw my face. He asked my brother and I to join him. He says every man in this band has a car. That meant that they were making money. Because there wasn't so many automobiles in those days I'm telling him. But we didn't want to go to Francisco. So I picked the job. And it was easy. I didn't have much to worry about except that I was featured every week. And who can't play I can't give anything but love on a trumpet for God's sake. And then every MC if you'll notice what they write on there, I was the one that said let's play this, let's play that. Because when Ray Teal came in there, he was my golfing competitor. When he was here. Well they all rocked. I played with everyone. Clyde Lucas, Rory Ballet and all the rest of them. They knew I had a call. I don't know. They liked me. I played trumpet. They knew me. I was one of them. And I could show them where the golf links were. We used to burlesque a lot. You know what I mean. Have a lot of fun. Clyde Lucas used to take his whole family with him when he'd go out. His brother and his father and all walk around. He'd meet a lot of nice people. I met Clyde afterwards at the convention with Jules Stein. Now you know who Jules Stein is. He's the head of MCA. Yeah. I know Mr. Stein very well. I said Mr. Stein what do you do to be a big band? I said I'm pretty big in my own town. He says I know that. Nothing. He said you bring your trumpet. I'll get you all the musicians and all the arrangers you want. Just bring your trumpet. You come. Now that's a nice offer huh. And with Jules Stein. So we're having lunch together in the hotel. I like the Blue Room. And there's one of those fiddle tenor bands up there. I said look at this. Look at that. The tenors are doing. Four tenors. Clyde Lucas says. Don't you think a week of this would push you to crazy house. Listen to that music. And that's one of Jules Stein's bands. Jules said listen Clyde. I make more money off of these kind of bands than I do off of your band. And I don't know if you're a band. I don't know if you're a band. I don't know if you're a band. I don't know if you're a band. They don't want to play in harmony. Yeah. And all those votes are not in the same position. You know that. Can they get up and make a speech about it? Mm-hm. Can he get up and make a speech about it? People will have the bad use of saying, I used to try to tell him not to say it, the public is stupid. The public is our living. The man that you make the most fun of, he got more money in his pocket than anybody in place. He pay every time you're playing on the court. It always developed that way. Not that we look for tips, but we never refused them. Only came in handy for the spaghetti and meatballs. We used to get off at 2 o'clock in the morning at the Edgewater, we'd stop at Fairchild and they'd open the kitchen for us. Because we'd stop there all the time. The guy didn't mind warming up, some leftover spaghetti, it tasted good. We were hungry, starving. But most of the time at the Edgewater, we were well fed. We had a drag with the cook, and I'd tell him we don't have much time. He'd give me a big piece of French bread, fresh, and put a filet mignon in there. I'll tell you what, the butter dripping over it, pickles, I'll tell you that was worse, better than that bag with those people who paid. I'll play the cook for Coca-Cola over there, I'll tell you about that, but the $900? They had over 900 people. And the man wanted the salad fresh. They never served 900 in their life in the Edgewater. How are they going to serve 900 salads? Where are they going to put them in the first place? They don't have the iceboxes. So by the time the people came in, it was wilted. And you know what I had to do? Just played them in. I played every college year that was ever written so I wouldn't miss anybody because you get drunk and punch you in the nose. You don't play at college. The guy come up to the market and said, play Bradley. And I made the mistake. I said, where is Bradley? Ooh, whoop! Where is Bradley? And one of the guys in the band said, that's the basketball team was caught cheating or something. Remember that Miss Cannon? And that was, I want to lick the band. I said, you don't listen. I said, we're kidding you. I said, whistle it to us. He whistled us, Bradley. We played a couple of bars. Because we could fake anything, some of us. And my piano player was a good figure too. He said, you knew Bradley, you didn't want to play.
I said, we all that shit.

We were friends. I remember when I was in one of those country towns, we just played the carnival ball and had the tabloid, we were tied a little bit, and it was my custom, after the carnival ball, to play one set and take another mission. So the band's on and I'm straightening up things. And some country hit comes up to me, where's the music, where's the music, where's the music, what do you mean? I paid to come in here. I said, I know you're paid to come in here. I said, we just got through playing the ball. I said, get the drink. I said, I'm going to get a beer. Will you have one? I bought him a beer and it was my friend for life. Just to show you, you've got to use diplomacy. I got sassy with that guy, I wouldn't have been able to blow the rest of the night, he popped me right in the mouth. But I said, I'm going to get the beer, come on, come with me. We go down and drink a couple of beers. He was my bodyguard all night. Up in the Balkan A's where I played, we had two prize fighters, floor managers, you know, they wore tuxedos. One was Chuck Connors, an ex-heavyweight prize fighter. And I was there, that year the World Series was in New York, and he says to me, you want to go to the World Series? I get you. And I was asking me. I said, sure. I said, meet him. I meet him at the Polar Grounds. He said, I can't find a guy. That wasn't that. He wanted me to take him into the boat. You know, into the boat. So I said, well that's all right, forget about it. I got the dough. I gave the guy ten bucks. It was three dollars a piece. He don't give any change. I said to the guy, is it ten dollars, five dollars a ticket? He said, no, it's three. I said, well, it's a change. Oh, I forgot. I said, if you average four dollars out of every ten dollars that comes into this window, you're going to have a good day, mister. New York is the most famous short change place in the world. People rush for the subway, give them all that change. Not me, I'm not giving a guy ten dollars when I know two tickets, only six dollars. And I saw the World Series, but the next day I didn't go take Chuck Connors, he didn't go find another sucker. And in fact a guy told me, weren't you at the polo grounds? I said, yeah, got a bad record. Pick him up, they might pick you up. But he was a bouncer in my time. Oh, I had a lot of experience. I had Jack Stone, the Australian middleweight, he gave me his picture and he said, although you are far from home, you can always depend on Jack Stone. And if he saw everybody get rambunctious near the bandstand, he'd come sidling up there and break it up.
Who was playing the World Series then? Do you remember?

Washington was one of the teams because the New Orleans boy Joe Martino pitched one in in while the great Matthews had somebody warmed up. Yeah that's why I was so interested in it because we had New Orleans pitchers to them. Sixty-five thousand people looking at the ball game. When that ball game was over I never saw so many people rush for the streetcars and what was a big shot and looked for a taxi cab. And I was just as hard to get into the streetcar. Taxi cab was about twenty cents a mile or something. Everything was cheap. I had wonderful experiences. Ask me something that's of interest to you though.
I'm just wondering if you ever played many things for churches, you know, you mentioned being a mason. For the Shriners? Yeah. Well I played the Muslim ball every year.

I played all the Masonic balls and many others that were not Masonic. I played Clough Knight Revelers, Proteus, Harlekins. I played on the average of thirty-five carnival balls a season. Get through at twelve o'clock and rush to the hotel and play one to four and then have rehearsal next morning, nine o'clock and everybody's knocked out and they're in a bad humor. Captain Donoghé, one note from the other. I used to have to tell them, who's the musician here, you or me? I can get enough of them. Then they say he's ornery. I played a show one night for the Kiwanis club and they had Al Streeman. Now I love Al, he's a great guy, nice fella. Musician, nothing. If you're doing an act, you'll have to be sitting on your music when they're caught when they're announced you. I played a show and the boys would ever suddenly thought it was an amateur show, they're taking it too easy. So I stopped and I said, this has to be professional. If it's never been done before, it's going to be done in a professional manner tonight. These people went in their introductions and they went in their company. So we got through, the man paid me. He said, Johnny, you're a great musician, but you're on the rails, Harry. Why?
Then he gives me a $100 tip.

And I took it, a $100 bail, I took it, it was a show with my pie. But he had to tell me that I was ornery. When I broadcast for posters on WDSU, I forget, I'm so seldom I have a broadcast. I couldn't get a mix, I couldn't get a test. Every time we were trying to tune up, I said, shh, somebody, I said, well, what are going to do, I'm going to do a broadcast after one, I don't even see a microphone. Because I had music go for 26 weeks and I would set it up myself. I'd see that everything was set to go over the air. I was working for Ballstaff, you know, nice job, 26 weeks. And only a half hour, you've done it quickly. We'd close the curtains and play in nice shirts, sweatshirts. Well because they didn't have any air conditioning. I've been talking about it. I didn't care, they could take all their clothes off, they blew the whole notes, nobody could see us. And I'm telling you, we're kind of bad conditions sometimes. I got to be on it for no reason at all. They brought in a script that long. I said, you're going to read that? They said, yeah. I said, nothing to do it. I said, why? He said, why? I said, if they don't know me now, when are they going to know me? That's recently, you know, I'm retired 11 years. I said, and the announcer, I forget who he is, but he's with the big time now. He said, that's an idea. So we went on to hear, he said, ladies and gentlemen, Holmes presents Johnny the director of his orchestra. He says, no use wasting a lot of time, we can use it for music. Because if you don't know Johnny now, you'll never know him. And that was it. And I went into my program. And I played my program. Ted was listening, Ted the mute? He said, Johnny was fine. I didn't try to put on a production because we only had time to play three numbers. But I liked to play stardust, and if I say so myself, I played it very well on the trumpet. And I would start it with the three pickups, no introduction. Listen to me, you know. Then I had my background like an organ. I predominated, but still I had assistants. You know what I mean? I remember Mrs. Steer, who was a teacher at Royal Eye. Do you know what Mrs. Steer, Ellen Steer? My sister come running into her and said, you want to hear a trumpet player? Come hear this guy. And it's me. She said, that's Johnny Deidre. That's my old friend. I was like, oh, bleh. And for my little novelty, I had a college boy and a college girl, both handsome. They danced the stardust. And the stars would flicker, you know. And that's all the production man. And I closed with blue skies. And gave each of my takeoff men a chance. That was my program. Right after that, we opened up with Somebody Loves Me. With the gestures. You ever see the man doing the gestures? Somebody loves me. I hope it's you. You know, you hold your hand out and you're in there. Yeah. And the boys did it fine. I was out there and they made me, because I could see myself in the monitor, you know. Well, that was out of the book that we did at the dancers. You know, we used to do novelty tunes at dancers, you know. And they all knew the words. Don't think, they didn't have to learn anything for that, for mistakes, you know what I mean? You don't want any mistakes on TV. You want it on, if you're only going to play jatter, play it. Play it right. So I picked out tunes. We knew Somebody Loves Me, and it was kind of an introduction. Somebody loves me, I hope it's you. You know, for me, for me. And I was singing, we'd say, we're all singing, we're doing the gestures. And it's just that if you're listening and you're seeing me, you see, I'm saying, somebody loves me and I hope it's you. It was a pretty fair, accidental introduction. Sounds fine. It sounds fine. And he made a little announcement. I did star rest. This couple came out, they looked splendid. They were dancing under the stars. They knew when the music stopped, they stopped. And they just walked off like a couple were walking. They didn't say anything, a bar like a couple of hams. I said, this is the dance, you're not doing an act. You just glide off.
And he took her on and walked off.

Papaya, to the contrary, wants to stress that he plays a lot of carnival balls. He brings up a lot of people with carnival costumes on and it's a motley mess with people falling all over and sitting in front of the band and look like a... Oh, no. I went for the artistic. But the only thing is, every time I want to get a ticket, test somebody was doing something else.
Well I said, the hell with you, I'm going to tune up. Hit the D minor chord, we're going to tune it again. I want that A, don't you want the A before you go on the air?

Oh yeah. I was the only band in town that never had to look around for musicians. When I picked the A kind of, the D minor chord on the piano, my band knew that's the time to come back on the bandstand. And nobody knew I was calling them. Because they thought I was tuning up, see. I go, and if they didn't come right away, they hit it hard, then they come, see. Because they had intermission, I didn't stop telling where they'd go, they'd see their friends, they'd go get a drink, a cup of coffee. But when they heard the D minor chord, they'd come back on. And I thought that was a good deal, don't you think? Oh yeah. I also had another deal that I cut it out. I got a lot of cheap batons with my name on it. And I used to accidentally lose them, you know, let them go. And the kids used to scramble for me. I thought it was a gag, don't you think so? Oh sure. I'm sure it worked for you. I said, I put on a merry Christmas, you've got to get drunk. All that helps. But you can't please everybody. You're playing for, a man will come up and give you a job, he's wanting to hire you for years, like Loyola alumni. He's 55, 60 years old. He knows Margie and high society and stuff like that. And he wants it. He gave you the engagement. You play it and some young punks, they want to put you down, you know? They want that job. They're even dancing. I said, you don't dance, you don't move. What are you complaining about? They're standing on one spot. They said, you know, can't you play some decent music? I would punch him in the nose. If I'd have been a big guy there'd have been a lot of broken noses around this town. I'd say they did fool with Blue Steel. You ever hear of Blue Steel?
I've heard about it.

He used to lick more people and get drunk. If you fool with him, he'd knock them down. And right here was the same type, about six foot straight old man, did his handball every morning, or played golf with me. He's the handsome man. Now he plays character parts, the most ugly parts. He looks like a big old fat sneaky sheriff or something like that. But he came here not long ago. When he phoned me, he was out on the driving range. He hit some balls after I went out to see him. I said, Ray, you're getting a little stout. He says, if I take the stomach off I don't get the part. I said, you compared yourself. He's like, stomach helps to get the part. He says, I'm not the leading man but I'm doing very well. There was a saxophone player, played a nice tone. He walked in there to stand up. He didn't know any of us. And he says, I would like to meet the arrangers. And we all started looking at one arrangers. He says, you don't have any arrangers? We didn't. We didn't have an arranger. We'd say let's play jazz and blues. And we'd play them and go on. I'd get up and take a chorus and friend and get up and take a chorus and the whole bag would come in on the last seat and the house would come down. We had the audience strained. They didn't have us strained. That's a fact. They just, and we had Lebowski up here. He was a wizard. Did you ever hear Lebowski? Only on record. He's great. His brother was a fine violinist too. Lebowski died early in life. He took $27,000 worth of insurance and about six months after they died. He went too long. But he must have had something wrong with his lawn. I liked him. He gave me a marvelous compliment on him when day is done. He was a good man. Oh, beautiful. And naturally when I bow I would point to Lebowski. He'd point to me, it's all you. You don't both would be hamming it up, you know. Well, that's for now. The first thing Ben Black told us, I'm very lenient. I'm not a great musician. I need your help. But I want you men to smile when a man's playing a solo as if he was your brother. Let all that petty hatred go up for tomorrow. When a man's taking off, he's great. Because if you don't reflect that he's great, the audience won't reflect it either. And in that band, 16 men, there were 16 jealousies. And they were all aimed at me. Because I was being paid the money. I was assisting the family. They didn't have the capability. When Ben Black got an iron giant and he couldn't talk, and somebody said, what about Johnny D. He'd write. Because I had been a leader all my life. I was just a side man that helped him work out that contract. And he said, Johnny, can you talk? I said, certainly. Am I talking? Can you announce the show? I said, surely. So I walk out and I say, ladies and gentlemen, due to the fact that Mr. Black has iron giant and can't speak, I've been asked to take over the show. The first act will be this. I didn't go into a long speech. First act will be Jones and Jones and something like that. Oh I'd say, so and so, I'd say, Singham. I said he was formerly with the Metropolitan Life Insurance Company. I'd get a laugh, you know. You know, a little carny joke and all that. Not too much. Don't make it long, see. Then if what Ben Black had picked out for the old show, I did a good wooden feature to me, I'd say, well Ben don't you think you ought to be down front with the horn? Because they're waiting all the time. When's he going to blow the horn? Yeah. So Ben says yes. Well I had to do that for Art Landry. You ever hear of Art Landry? Yes.
Well he was a hop hit.

In the old man. You know, he couldn't get it, he collapsed. Throw a shoe in my lap. Well I'll play one of them. What do you think I played? Two-inch swing. With all the variations. He comes back next week, he says, well you had Johnny last week and I understand you liked him. But Johnny only records for okay. I'm going to get him with Victor. He's going to get me with Victor. He better get himself a doctor. But jealousy. We fell out entirely. I moved out of there, went up to Stran. I played in Stran. Where was Art Landry from? God knows.
He had a false mustache. He painted on him.

He got sore with me for no reason. He said he was a golf player. So we took him out. I think CUNY was in the force. I mean CUNY, I told you he was a 135 pound champion wrestler. Great guy, feared nobody. And Landry kept borrowing golf balls which you don't find the street. And he knocks a few over the fence. So CUNY says, excuse me Mr. Landry, those are my golf balls you're knocking over the fence. I mean, out of bounds. You know what golf is. You play golf. So a kid comes along with a hat full of balls. And I said, hey Landry, he's got a hat full of balls. I said, tell him to his face. I don't face you. You're not getting any of my golf balls, I'll tell you that. I went and he says, how much? The kid says, three dollars. And he says, I'm going to get a bar on golf balls. And he's got a bar on golf balls, which you don't find the street. And he knocks a few over the fence. So CUNY says, excuse me Mr. Landry, those are my golf balls you're knocking over the fence. You know? I mean, out of bounds. You know what golf is. You play golf.
So a kid comes along with a hat full of balls.

And I said, hey Landry, this guy with a hat full of balls. I said, tell him to his face. I don't face you, it's not getting any of my golf balls, I'll tell you that. I went and he says, how much? He says, three dollars. He says, lend me three dollars. He said, no money. I loaned him three dollars. Now I didn't like him too much. And I know he didn't like me. I waited for my three bucks. So one day I go up in his office and he's got a couple in there. I always talk to him. I said, Mr. Landry, haven't you forgotten that you owe me three dollars? He says, sirs. He says, I thought you needed it. I said, I didn't need it as much you needed as though the golf links. That's all I said to him. He thought I needed it after he wasn't going to pay me.
Three dollars didn't mean anything.

I'm making around nearly two hundred after you had extras. If there was any extra money I got it. If one of the places they blew his blues, he said, let Johnny play a chorus, it'll help my organ solo. You know what I mean? The organ used to go up. You know how to do it. And I'd come out of the alcove and put the derby and go in the St. Louis booth. I used to get all the extras. We used to do a radio program for a half hour. I used to get that. Ray McNamara, just Ray McNamara. He played the piano and I played the piano. We'd pick out some numbers that everybody wanted to use. And the other guys that'd be playing putt-putt knocking us, telling us Tom Lousey, they said, you have a putt-putt place to cross the same.
Did Ray McNamara ever write any tunes?

He was going to ask you, I could get your checks with him. Sure. He was Pinky Vodakovich. Remember Pinky? Sure. Pinky was a clever boy. Not much of a musician, but very clever. I brought him over to Bluxley to play a strip. We had a ball, the title of which was Shrimp Boats. They always said, Johnny, you're in New Orleans, you're getting more entertainment. Get us some entertainment. So I said, well now Pinky would be ideal because he has that accent. He's from down in Buras, you know. So Pinky comes over there dressed like a shrimp fisherman. He wouldn't dress. Faded dungarees, a blue turtleneck sweater, and a knitted cap. I guess they thought he was some bum, but he was dressed in character. And he tells these boogaloo jokes, and the people in Biloxi don't talk that way. They don't know anything about the Cajun language. No. No, they don't. They're shrimp pickers. But this ball wasn't shrimp pickers. It was a high class ball because they wouldn't have had that kind of money. I gave Pinky a hundred bucks to do it in about five minutes. And he's dying out there. I said, it's the wrong thing. I broke the wrong thing. So he looks at me, I said, sing. He says, all right folks, I'm going to sing my own composition, Arizay. You remember he wrote Arizay? Sure. And my piano player says, where's the music? Pinky comes in with our music, of all people, our band. But the band knew Arizay, so we went into Arizay and we played it for him. Piano player faked up and we're keeping all that good time, you're listening to all that
foolishness. Well that's the kind of stuff we want. I'm just worried the tape's going to run out in the middle of it, that's all.
Oh I can tell you a whole lot of things. Foolish things.
Well I thought you recorded one of McNamara's tunes is the reason I asked.

Oh yeah, I made it, Nobody Knows Blues. Nobody knows, nobody knows. I've been on a tune too, I have a third of them. Three of us. Jimmy Dupree, Ray McNamara. Well did Jimmy Dupree write words or music or what? Oh he had a million tunes.
I bought a half interest in many tunes just to get it off my back.

Because he was always, he'd steal an orchestration of Dave Frank and sell it to me. He came over to Biloxi when someone was playing at the Buena Vista and he puts his head in the door and he says, hey Pops. Oh I said, my God, I got this guy on my hands all summer. He came in with his clothes wrapped in the newspaper. But I wasn't eating in the hotel because I had taken a cottage because I was expecting visitors. So I told him, I said I'm entitled to three meals a day. I said please give them to this fellow. So Jimmy Dupree ate his three meals a day in the Buena Vista for free. And Fazola, the gang, took him up to an apartment they had and he slept in the bathtub. He was a bum. I said, won't you sing a song, one song for God's sake, do something for me. When the band stands, he could sing a little bit you know. I had a bunch, I had four guys in my band, played more music for nothing than they played for money. After we get through at 12 o'clock I could hear them out in the Gulf of Mexico playing on somebody's job. The drummer had a five gallon can and a couple of swatters. Fazola had his clarinet. And Skaglione had his altitude, that's a man he should have met. He died with me when I was at the jump, he died of cancer. They cut him open and closed him right away. And he was stout and he used to sweat in the coldest weather. And I used to think that he was lazy. I said you just don't want to wake. Johnny I'm suffering. He didn't suffer to me. Well one day he didn't show up. I think we got Maia Weinberg. That's when I got Maia. Maia used to kill me. He used to come to rehearsal dressed like an elephant hunter. He got a job and a puzzle on. He stuck on the girl singer I had there, bringing the flowers. He moved out to the oil station, man, 35 bucks. I said, mister I don't owe you a nickel. You go find Maia Weinberg. He said, where's that Maia Weinberg? I said, I don't know if he's doing anything about it. He's gone. I had two men in my band. I had a salary going to sheath. I had to write checks for him. I had to job. That's when I got Ray Teal a job. I had to job at the job. I was a leader. But they start changing bands, name bands. And I wanted to job. It was a nice job. So I told the manager, his name was Jimmy Lynch, that time. I said, you don't have to change band. I said, you bring a name band and it's going to cost you an awful lot of money. I said, I'll get you a name leader, Ray Teal. I said, you just build up the fact that Ray Teal has been master ceremonies at the Sanger. And we'll make something out of it. See? So I wrote Ray. And Ray was trooping around with a company. He had only five men in the orchestra. I believe he had a drum, a piano, two trumpets and a trombone. Must have been a lot. But he said it sounded good. I guess five good men in any instrumentation. If they could. But when he came down, I noticed he had a linen suit and it was all frayed in the back. He must have been on the hall. He must have been. So we wore tuxedos that looked at him. And he wore a full red suit. And he said to me, Johnny, you want to get some good tuxedo shirts cheap? I said, where? He says, at the Junior League rummage sale. He bought his shirts at the rummage sale. Can you imagine? Bought his full red suits at the rummage sale. He must have been on the hall, yeah? On the bum, huh? He must have been. And I want to tell you, prior to opening, he went around listening to other bands. I said, why are you listening to other bands? You're going to use my band. If you don't, I said, I'm going to the union, see that you don't play at all. Because Orn Tucker, you heard of Orn Tucker? Sure.
He came down here.

segments.title: Opening chatter: Burt Andrews, Souchon's book and the jazz club
segments.summary: DeDroit settles in at home; he mentions Burt Andrews, Dutch's brother, left out of Souchon's book, and his lapsed membership in the jazz club.

segments.title: Name, family naming and French heritage; introductions for the tape
segments.summary: He gives his full name, explains the John and Paul names in the family and the French spoken around him, and everyone states their name for the tape.

segments.title: His brother Paul, drummer and sound-effects man in Hollywood
segments.summary: DeDroit describes his brother Paul, a drummer and marimba player who worked with Alfred Newman and later in cartoon sound effects.

segments.title: Violin, piano and trumpet lessons with Paulin Fabian
segments.summary: He played violin well enough to double, studied trumpet with a former Republican Guard Band musician, and earned $8 at his first engagement at 12.

segments.title: Birthday, his wife's long illness and living in the Georgian
segments.summary: They note his birthday, and he talks about caring for his sick wife for four years, her death, Medicare, his daughter and the friends around him.

segments.chapter: Early career, theaters and Cobb's Tea Room
segments.title: Born in New Orleans; touring with Arnold Johnson and playing the Grunewald
segments.summary: He recounts touring as Arnold Johnson under Paul Whiteman's name after Atlantic City, then the cave at the Grunewald where Fazola played with him.

segments.chapter: Early career, theaters and Cobb's Tea Room
segments.title: Summer jobs at the Buena Vista in Biloxi
segments.summary: He describes the summer engagements at Biloxi hotels and their perks, and regrets the hurricane damage there.

segments.chapter: Early career, theaters and Cobb's Tea Room
segments.title: His father the bandmaster, and DeDroit's poor memory for dates
segments.summary: His father led a Spanish-American War regimental band and later ran a store; DeDroit says he remembers tunes better than dates.

segments.chapter: Early career, theaters and Cobb's Tea Room
segments.title: First trumpet, hearing Brunies in Biloxi, and the Alamo theater pit under Tasso
segments.summary: His father gave him a trumpet at ten; he recalls hearing Abbie and Merritt Brunies, playing the symphony, and his muted trumpet feature in the Alamo pit, praised in the press.

segments.chapter: Early career, theaters and Cobb's Tea Room
segments.title: Directing silent-film scores at the Liberty Theater
segments.summary: As leader of the Liberty Theater orchestra he played feature pictures for the first thirty minutes and says he worked steadily for eleven years.

segments.chapter: Early career, theaters and Cobb's Tea Room
segments.title: Four years at the Grunewald and seven years at Cobb's Tea Room
segments.summary: He explains how he persuaded Mr. Cobb to open the tea room, drew his own following and effectively ran the place without a contract.

segments.chapter: Early career, theaters and Cobb's Tea Room
segments.title: Trumpeter Frank Garante and his rotary-valve trumpet
segments.summary: Allen asks about Frank Garante; DeDroit says they played duets and describes his Italian rotary-valve trumpet.

segments.chapter: Early career, theaters and Cobb's Tea Room
segments.title: Hustling for work and his wife's resentment (partly off the record)
segments.summary: DeDroit talks about working lunch, dinner and night sessions while his wife complained of his absence; he asks that something personal be cut.

segments.chapter: Early career, theaters and Cobb's Tea Room
segments.title: Meeting his wife, his daughter and his wife as band leader's partner in Biloxi
segments.summary: He recalls meeting his wife at 14, her illnesses, his daughter and granddaughter, and her poise at Biloxi dances.

segments.title: Armistice Day and piano player Tom Zimmerman
segments.summary: On Armistice Day the Grunewald manager asked for the band at noon; his wife filled in on piano, and he praises pianist Tom Zimmerman.

segments.title: Clarence Williams's tunes in New York and the sidemen of his band
segments.summary: He recalls Clarence Williams bringing him tunes at Healy's, his impeccable band's look, and sidemen like Meyer Weinberg, Joe Loyacano, Eddie Powers and Almerico.

segments.title: Wyatt Sharp and Jerry Lane, the riverboat captain and MCA price bids
segments.summary: One long answer covers Wyatt Sharp's hotel trick, running a band on the boat against the captain's wishes, and how MCA bids undercut him.

segments.title: MCA, the Edgewater, and standing up to a maitre d'
segments.summary: He says MCA sent worse bands for pay, praises the Edgewater's manager and Seymour Weiss, and tells of threatening an insolent maitre d'.

segments.title: Protege sidemen Charlie Luckow and Bob Young
segments.summary: He speaks of auditioning Charlie Luckow, taking sax man Bob Young into the union at 16, and Bob's health.

segments.title: Floor shows, Dick Shawn, Russ Papalia and Billy DeWolf
segments.summary: He tells of playing for Dick Shawn and others, using trombonist Russ Papalia as his substitute, and a joke from Billy DeWolf and a critic's review.

segments.title: Records and Mr. Peer of OKeh
segments.summary: Asked about Russ Papalia on his records, he says nothing distinguished his records and begins a story about OKeh's Mr. Peer and a golf game.

segments.title: Falling out with Souchon over his book
segments.summary: After a pause, he explains how his remark to Souchon strained their friendship and how the book slighted his brother, though he says he was wrong.

segments.title: Chicago: the Green Mill Gardens audition, Isham Jones and Vic Berton
segments.summary: He recounts sitting in at the Chicago club, getting the job, Isham Jones's interest and drummer Vic Berton; the long answer also covers his finances and being named a jazz model.

segments.title: Los Angeles with his brother, being a has-been, and today's New Orleans bands
segments.summary: He describes the Hollywood musicians' clique and Frank Segrest, then comments on the Dixieland band on Bourbon Street, Raymond Burke, Alvin Alcorn and the trombonist.

segments.title: Eating alone in New Orleans and Miami Beach
segments.summary: He talks about his lonely meals in New Orleans and the restaurants of Miami Beach.

segments.title: The Tango Belt and playing with Black bands in the district
segments.summary: Asked about the Tango Belt, he says he did not play there but visited district joints with his brother, playing with Black bands.

segments.title: Professor Robichaux, A. J. Piron and the competing dance spots
segments.summary: He recalls the left-handed violinist Robichaux, Piron's orchestra at Tranchina's, and the rival spots such as the halfway house.

segments.title: Johnny Bayersdorffer, the best Dixieland trumpeter
segments.summary: He praises Johnny Bayersdorffer as his idea of a clean Dixieland trumpet, whose OKeh recordings he thinks the best, and says he never got his due.

segments.title: Band loyalty, bassist Dan LeBlanc and guitarist Arthur Ponce
segments.summary: He talks about taking any work to keep the men employed, bassist Dan LeBlanc, and guitarist Arthur Ponce, a phone call, and Ponce's arrangements.

segments.title: Ponce's night in jail, Bob Young, spaghetti suppers and Perretti at the Liberty
segments.summary: One long answer covers Ponce's arrest, fishing with Bob Young, the band's spaghetti suppers, Perretti's betting, and taking over the Liberty pit from Max Fink.

segments.chapter: Theater broadcasts, recordings and the road
segments.title: Poet and Peasant overture and the first good radio broadcast from the Liberty
segments.summary: He tells how he played Poet and Peasant on trumpet to win over the Liberty, and of the early broadcast with thirteen men and a soprano.

segments.chapter: Theater broadcasts, recordings and the road
segments.title: Why the New York and New Orleans recordings sound different; studio dubbing
segments.summary: Asked about the band's sound, he says New York used studio men and describes how film studios dub and time music to pictures.

segments.chapter: Theater broadcasts, recordings and the road
segments.title: Tuba player Barney Aquilino, the six-day bicycle race and Vincent Lopez
segments.summary: He tells how a charity bicycle-race job led to Vincent Lopez's management, his $75 weekly contract and recording fees, and theatergoing in New York.

segments.chapter: Theater broadcasts, recordings and the road
segments.title: Charlie Whittaker, Jack Benny, Al Jolson and recording with Frisco
segments.summary: He recalls friends in New York theater circles, being asked by Jolson to fill breaks, and recordings with Johnson on Brunswick.

segments.chapter: Theater broadcasts, recordings and the road
segments.title: Vaudeville tour with Adelaide Hughes and pasting orchestrations together
segments.summary: He describes joining a vaudeville act as a trumpet feature, improvising by combining stock orchestrations, and playing next to Eisenhower.

segments.chapter: Theater broadcasts, recordings and the road
segments.title: Houston's Rice Hotel and the rival trumpeter's polish
segments.summary: He tells of a night on the Rice Hotel roof in Houston, being left to fill the job, and the can of metal polish.

segments.chapter: Theater broadcasts, recordings and the road
segments.title: Wartime bands, the Interstate show, Cobb's split-week acts and the Rampart Street Parade
segments.summary: One long answer covers touring in the war, booking acts at Cobb's, Mr. Cobb's generosity and his opinion of the Rampart Street Parade.

segments.chapter: Theater broadcasts, recordings and the road
segments.title: Drummers Raymond Baduc and Monk Hazel; talk about the tape
segments.summary: He discusses Raymond Baduc subbing at Cobb's, the drummer Monk Hazel, and then the tape-recording arrangements.

segments.title: Break: refreshments and housekeeping
segments.summary: The interview pauses for drinks and chatter about housekeeping.

segments.title: Taking a lady to dinner, living alone, and being interviewed
segments.summary: He tells of dining with a new friend after his wife's death and Allen says the stories are fascinating.

segments.title: Odd engagements: Picayune, a bad piano and Frank Curety
segments.summary: He recounts playing in decrepit halls, and pianist Frank Curety who tuned pianos and played the phantom bass.

segments.title: Playing school and convent dances; Al Black sings I Believe
segments.summary: He explains how he behaved as a gentleman at Gulf Coast schools and convents, and singer Al Black's number.

segments.title: Hiring trumpeter Al Blanco and the Donaldsonville Fair
segments.summary: He tells how he heard Blanco at a jam session, took him on, and played the Donaldsonville Fair for Huey Long.

segments.title: Arnold Johnson: ensemble only and the Hamilton, Ontario dance
segments.summary: Asked about choruses on Arnold Johnson records, he says he played only ensembles and tells of the Hamilton dance.

segments.title: English breakfast in Hamilton, a trip to Europe and pronouncing his name
segments.summary: Continuing the Hamilton story, he talks about wanting to visit London and the pronunciation of DeDroit.

segments.title: Rudolph Levy, trumpet lessons with Fabian and the Arban method, health and age
segments.summary: He mentions a former saxophonist's visit, the Arban method taught by Fabian, bronchitis and his habits and age.

segments.title: His mother, pictures and clothes at home
segments.summary: He talks about his mother who lived to 94, a Venice painting, a photo of his brother and his clothes.

segments.chapter: Sanger, Ben Black and carnival balls
segments.title: Letter to Nick LaRocca and teaching him to read music
segments.summary: He reads his letter to LaRocca and recalls teaching him to scale on the pool-room blackboard.

segments.chapter: Sanger, Ben Black and carnival balls
segments.title: The Strand, St. Charles, the Sanger and Ben Black, Jules Stein, the Edgewater
segments.summary: One long answer covers the Strand pit, a St. Charles contract, the Sanger side-man job under Ben Black, MCA's Jules Stein and a convention.

segments.chapter: Sanger, Ben Black and carnival balls
segments.title: Keeping peace at dances, bouncer Chuck Connors and the World Series
segments.summary: He tells of buying a beer to defuse an angry patron, prize-fighter floor managers in New York and a World Series game.

segments.chapter: Sanger, Ben Black and carnival balls
segments.title: Playing carnival balls and a Kiwanis show
segments.summary: He says he played thirty-five carnival balls a season and recounts a Kiwanis show he insisted on running professionally.

segments.chapter: Sanger, Ben Black and carnival balls

segments.summary: He describes his broadcast and TV program, announcing himself, playing Stardust and Blue Skies with dancers.

segments.summary: He explains tuning up as a signal for the band, giving away batons, and handling critical customers.
